content.stem: Ultrasonic testing uses:
options: High-frequency sound waves to detect flaws and measure thickness
Low-frequency sound waves sitting below the range of human hearing
Sound waves that pass only through the open air around the part
A steady continuous tone instead of the short pulses of sound used
content.explanation: UT introduces high-frequency sound into a material and uses the returning echoes to find discontinuities and measure thickness.
distractors: UT uses high-frequency sound above hearing, not below it.
UT sound travels through the part, not only through air.
Pulse-echo UT uses short pulses, not a continuous tone.

content.stem: Sound waves require:
options: A medium (solid, liquid, or gas) to travel through
Nothing at all, since it passes through a vacuum freely
A source of light present to carry it along its path
An electromagnetic field in order to radiate outward
content.explanation: Sound is a mechanical vibration that needs a medium to propagate; it cannot travel through a vacuum.
distractors: Sound cannot travel through a vacuum.
Sound does not require light to propagate.
Sound is mechanical, not a form of radiation.

content.stem: Ultrasonic frequencies are those:
options: Above the range of human hearing (above about 20 kHz)
Below the range of human hearing (under about 20 Hz only)
Right within the normal range of everyday human speech
Up in the electromagnetic radio band of the spectrum
content.explanation: Ultrasound is sound above human hearing (above roughly 20 kHz). Industrial UT commonly uses frequencies from about 1 to 10 MHz.
distractors: Below 20 Hz is infrasound, not ultrasound.
Normal speech is within the audible range.
Radio waves are electromagnetic, not sound.

content.stem: Industrial UT commonly uses frequencies in the range of about:
options: 1 to 10 MHz
1 to 10 Hz
1 to 10 kHz
1 to 10 GHz
content.explanation: Most conventional UT is performed between roughly 1 and 10 MHz, balancing penetration and resolution. The exact frequency is chosen for the application.
distractors: 1 to 10 Hz is far below ultrasonic frequencies.
1 to 10 kHz is below the typical UT range.
1 to 10 GHz is far above conventional UT frequencies.

content.stem: Velocity, frequency, and wavelength are related by:
options: Velocity equals frequency times wavelength
Velocity equals frequency over the wavelength
Wavelength equals velocity times frequency
Velocity is fixed and ignores both of them
content.explanation: Velocity equals frequency times wavelength. For a fixed material velocity, raising the frequency shortens the wavelength.
distractors: Velocity is frequency times wavelength, not divided by it.
That inverts the relationship; velocity is frequency times wavelength.
Velocity is directly related to frequency and wavelength.

content.stem: The velocity of sound in a given material is mainly a property of:
options: The material and wave mode
The chosen test frequency
The pulse repetition rate
The set pulse amplitude
content.explanation: Sound velocity is set by the material and the wave mode (longitudinal, shear, surface), not by the chosen test frequency.
distractors: Frequency does not change the material's sound velocity.
Pulse repetition rate sets how often pulses are sent, not the velocity in the part.
Pulse amplitude affects signal strength, not the sound velocity.

content.stem: In a longitudinal (compression) wave, particle motion is:
options: Parallel to the direction of wave travel
Perpendicular to the direction of wave travel
Confined to a thin layer at the free surface
Absent, with no real particle movement at all
content.explanation: Longitudinal waves vibrate particles back and forth along the propagation direction. They travel in solids, liquids, and gases and are the fastest mode.
distractors: Perpendicular motion describes shear waves.
Surface-only motion describes surface (Rayleigh) waves.
A propagating wave involves particle motion.

content.stem: In a shear (transverse) wave, particle motion is:
options: Perpendicular to the direction of wave travel
Running parallel to the direction of wave travel
Elliptical, confined to the free surface layer
Absent, since no particle movement occurs at all
content.explanation: Shear waves vibrate particles across the propagation direction. They travel only in solids and move at roughly half the longitudinal velocity in the same material.
distractors: Parallel motion describes longitudinal waves.
Circular/elliptical surface motion describes Rayleigh waves.
A shear wave does involve particle motion.

content.stem: Shear waves can travel through:
options: Solids, but generally not liquids or gases
Liquids and gases just as well as it does solids
Gases more readily than through any solid metal
A vacuum as easily as it crosses a solid
content.explanation: Shear waves require a medium that supports shear stress, so they travel in solids but not in liquids or gases.
distractors: Shear waves do not propagate in liquids or gases as they do in solids.
Shear waves do not travel through gases.
No mechanical wave travels through a vacuum.

content.stem: Compared with the longitudinal velocity in the same steel, the shear velocity is about:
options: Roughly half
About equal
About double
Roughly tenfold
content.explanation: In steel the shear velocity is roughly half the longitudinal velocity, closer to about 0.55 times it. The half value is an approximation used at Level I, and it matters when setting up shear (angle-beam) inspections.
distractors: Shear velocity is lower, not equal, to longitudinal.
Shear velocity is lower, not double.
Shear velocity is not ten times the longitudinal velocity.

content.stem: A surface (Rayleigh) wave travels:
options: Along the surface to a depth of roughly one wavelength
Right through the center of the part along its axis
Through the body of a liquid bath surrounding the part
Faster than any longitudinal wave through the same metal
content.explanation: Surface waves follow the surface, penetrating on the order of one wavelength deep as an approximation, and are useful for surface and near-surface flaws on a part.
distractors: Surface waves follow the surface rather than the center.
Surface waves travel on solid surfaces, not in liquids.
Surface waves are slower than longitudinal waves.

content.stem: If material velocity is fixed, increasing the test frequency:
options: Shortens the wavelength
Lengthens the wavelength
Leaves it fully unchanged
Raises the sound velocity
content.explanation: Since velocity equals frequency times wavelength, raising frequency at a fixed velocity shortens the wavelength, which improves resolution of small flaws.
distractors: Higher frequency shortens, not lengthens, the wavelength.
Frequency does change the wavelength at fixed velocity.
Frequency does not change the material's velocity.

content.stem: In the pulse-echo technique, one transducer:
options: Sends a pulse and receives the returning echoes
Only receives, while a second one sends the pulse
Only sends, while a second one takes the echoes
Emits a short burst of X-rays toward the back wall
content.explanation: In pulse-echo, a single transducer transmits a sound pulse and then receives the echoes from reflectors and the back surface; the time of flight gives distance.
distractors: In pulse-echo the same transducer also receives.
In pulse-echo the same transducer also sends.
Transducers emit sound, not X-rays.

content.stem: Pulse-echo measures distance to a reflector using:
options: The travel time of the echo and the material velocity
The amplitude of the echo and the set receiver gain
The test frequency and the width of the probe crystal
The pulse repetition rate set on the instrument dial
content.explanation: Distance is found from the echo travel time and the known sound velocity in the material. Half the round-trip time corresponds to the one-way depth.
distractors: Amplitude relates to reflector size and orientation, not the distance.
Frequency affects resolution and penetration, not the distance calculation.
Pulse repetition rate is how often pulses fire, not how distance is measured.

content.stem: Through-transmission testing uses:
options: A separate transmitter and receiver on opposite sides
One single transducer that both sends and receives
Two probes set side by side on the very same face
The very same probe moved across to each side in turn
content.explanation: Through-transmission places a transmitting transducer on one side and a receiver on the other; a flaw reduces the received signal. It does not locate depth as pulse-echo does.
distractors: Using one transducer for both is pulse-echo, not through-transmission.
Through-transmission uses opposite faces, not the same face.
Two separate probes are used at once, not one moved about.

content.stem: Sound reflects at an interface when there is a difference in:
options: Acoustic impedance between the two materials
The surface color between the two materials
The hardness difference between the two materials
Electrical resistance between the two materials
content.explanation: Reflection occurs at boundaries where acoustic impedance changes. The larger the impedance mismatch, the more sound is reflected.
distractors: Color does not govern acoustic reflection.
Reflection depends on acoustic impedance, not hardness.
Electrical resistance does not govern sound reflection.

content.stem: Acoustic impedance is the product of a material's:
options: Density and sound velocity
Hardness and surface color
Weight and the temperature
Frequency and set gain
content.explanation: Acoustic impedance equals density times sound velocity. Impedance differences at interfaces determine how much sound reflects.
distractors: Hardness and color do not define acoustic impedance.
Weight and temperature do not define acoustic impedance.
Frequency and gain are instrument settings, not material impedance.

content.stem: An air gap between the transducer and the part reflects nearly all the sound because:
options: Air has a very large impedance mismatch with solids
Air carries the sound perfectly straight into the solid
Air is nonmagnetic, which blocks the sound at the gap
Air is optically clear, so the sound cannot cross it
content.explanation: The huge impedance difference between air and a solid reflects almost all the sound at the interface, which is why a couplant is needed to exclude air.
distractors: Air transmits sound poorly into solids, it does not conduct it perfectly.
Air is not magnetic, and that is irrelevant to sound transmission.
Optical transparency has nothing to do with sound transmission.

content.stem: A couplant is used in contact UT to:
options: Exclude air and transmit sound into the part
Stick the probe firmly onto the part surface
Cool the crystal down during a long scanning run
Color the indications so that they stand out
content.explanation: Couplant fills the gap between transducer and part, excluding air so sound can pass into the material efficiently.
distractors: Couplant transmits sound; it does not bond the probe on.
Couplant's main role is sound transmission, not cooling.
Couplant does not color indications.

content.stem: Attenuation is the:
options: Loss of sound energy as it travels through material
Amplification of the signal added in by the receiver
The echo returned from the back surface of the part
The speed at which the sound travels through the part
content.explanation: Attenuation is the weakening of the sound beam with distance, from absorption and scattering. It limits how deep flaws can be detected.
distractors: Gain is instrument amplification, the opposite of attenuation.
Backwall reflection is an echo, not the gradual energy loss called attenuation.
Speed of sound is velocity, a different property from attenuation.

content.stem: Attenuation is mainly caused by:
options: Absorption and scattering
Refraction at interfaces
The receiver gain setting
The delay zero setting
content.explanation: Sound energy is lost to absorption (conversion to heat) and scattering (deflection by grains and structure). Coarse grain increases scattering.
distractors: Refraction bends the beam at interfaces but is not the main cause of energy loss with distance.
Gain amplifies the signal; it does not cause the material attenuation.
The delay setting shifts the sweep zero; it does not cause attenuation.

content.stem: Coarse-grained material tends to:
options: Scatter sound and increase attenuation
Remove all attenuation and clear the noise
Speed up the instrument's entire sweep rate
Do away with the need for any couplant
content.explanation: Large grains scatter the beam, raising attenuation and noise, which often calls for lower frequencies to penetrate such material.
distractors: Coarse grain increases, not eliminates, attenuation.
Grain size does not speed up the instrument.
Couplant is still required regardless of grain size.

content.stem: Compared with lower frequencies, higher frequencies generally provide:
options: Better resolution and sensitivity to small flaws
More penetration through thick attenuative material
Lower attenuation right across the entire sound path
A longer wavelength at the same sound velocity
content.explanation: Higher frequency means shorter wavelength, improving resolution and small-flaw sensitivity, but with more attenuation and less penetration.
distractors: Higher frequency penetrates less, not more.
Higher frequency increases, not decreases, attenuation.
Higher frequency gives a shorter, not longer, wavelength.

content.stem: Lower frequencies are often chosen for:
options: Greater penetration in thick or attenuative material
Sharper resolution of the very small near-surface flaws
A shorter wavelength at the same sound velocity
A clear drop in attenuation across a coarse-grained part
content.explanation: Lower frequency penetrates deeper and is less affected by scattering, useful for thick or coarse-grained parts, at the cost of resolution.
distractors: Small-flaw resolution improves with higher, not lower, frequency.
Lower frequency gives a longer, not shorter, wavelength.
Lower frequency reduces, not raises, attenuation effects.

content.stem: Echo amplitude from a reflector depends partly on its:
options: Size, orientation, and the sound reaching it
The surface color of the reflector face itself
The overall weight of the reflector metal itself
The electrical charge held on the reflector
content.explanation: A larger reflector well-oriented to the beam and reached by adequate sound returns a stronger echo. Orientation strongly affects amplitude.
distractors: Reflector color does not affect echo amplitude.
Echo depends on size and orientation, not weight.
Electrical charge does not govern the echo amplitude.

content.stem: A planar flaw returns the strongest echo when it is:
options: Oriented roughly perpendicular to the sound beam
Lying roughly parallel to the path of the sound beam
Pressed tightly shut with its faces held in contact
Located very deep beneath the surface of the part
content.explanation: A flaw facing the beam reflects sound back to the transducer most strongly. A flaw nearly parallel to the beam may reflect little and be missed.
distractors: A flaw parallel to the beam reflects little back to the transducer.
A tight closed flaw reflects less; orientation drives echo strength.
Orientation to the beam matters most here, not depth.

content.stem: The back surface of a part produces a:
options: Backwall echo on the display
A color shift on the display
A flat dead line on the display
A complete loss of the signal
content.explanation: Sound reflecting off the far surface returns a backwall echo, used to confirm sound passed through and to set up thickness and calibration.
distractors: The backwall returns an echo, not a color change.
The back surface returns an echo, not a flat line.
The back surface reflects sound back, not loses it.

content.stem: A sudden loss of the backwall echo can indicate:
options: A reflector or condition redirecting or absorbing the sound
A perfectly sound part, proving no flaw is present at all
A dead instrument that has simply stopped working entirely
A color change appearing right across the display screen
content.explanation: Losing the backwall may mean a large flaw, a lamination, heavy attenuation, or poor coupling is interrupting the sound path, which the technician investigates.
distractors: Loss of backwall is a signal to investigate, not proof of perfect material.
It is not necessarily a dead instrument; coupling and flaws must be checked.
Backwall loss is an acoustic effect, not a color change.

content.stem: The common ultrasonic wave modes used in UT are:
options: Longitudinal, shear, and surface
Longitudinal waves and nothing else
Radio, microwave, and the infrared
Bending, twisting, and tension waves
content.explanation: Conventional UT uses longitudinal, shear, and surface waves. Straight-beam work is usually longitudinal; angle-beam work is usually shear.
distractors: More than longitudinal waves are used; shear and surface modes are common.
Radio and microwave are electromagnetic, not ultrasonic modes.
Those are mechanical load terms, not ultrasonic wave modes.

content.stem: Of the common modes in a given solid, the fastest is the:
options: Longitudinal wave
The shear wave
The surface wave
They are all equal
content.explanation: Longitudinal waves travel fastest, shear waves at roughly half that speed, and surface waves slightly slower than shear.
distractors: Shear waves are slower than longitudinal.
Surface waves are slower than shear and longitudinal.
The modes have different velocities, not equal ones.

content.stem: Two common uses of UT are:
options: Detecting internal flaws and measuring thickness
Measuring the weight and the color of the part
Measuring the surface hardness and the grain size
Recording the surface roughness over the entire part
content.explanation: UT is widely used to find internal and surface-connected flaws and to measure remaining wall thickness, among other applications.
distractors: UT does not measure weight or color.
UT finds flaws and measures thickness; it does not test hardness.
UT measures thickness and finds flaws, not surface roughness.

content.stem: Unlike MT and PT, UT can detect:
options: Flaws deep within the volume of a part
Only the flaws right at the outer surface
Flaws in magnetic materials only
Color changes across the part's surface
content.explanation: UT is a volumetric method that can find internal flaws at depth, not just surface or near-surface conditions.
distractors: UT is not limited to surface flaws.
UT works on nonmagnetic materials too, not only magnetic ones.
UT detects acoustic reflectors, not color changes.

content.stem: Detectable flaw size is generally related to wavelength such that smaller flaws need:
options: Shorter wavelengths (higher frequency)
Longer wavelengths (a lower frequency)
No sound at all, only a steady field
A much lower test frequency than usual
content.explanation: As a rule of thumb, flaws much smaller than the wavelength are hard to detect, so smaller flaws call for shorter wavelengths (higher frequency).
distractors: Longer wavelengths detect small flaws less well.
Sound is required to detect flaws.
Lower frequency gives longer wavelengths, reducing small-flaw detection.

content.stem: Sound velocity in aluminum versus steel is:
options: Different, because velocity depends on the material
Exactly the same in both of those two metals
Zero, since sound cannot move through solids
Set by the instrument and not by the metal itself
content.explanation: Each material has its own sound velocity, so calibration and thickness readings must use the correct velocity for the material being tested.
distractors: Velocities differ between materials.
Velocity is not zero in solids.
The instrument does not set the material velocity; the material does.

content.stem: A couplant works partly by providing an acoustic path with impedance:
options: Higher than air, so it excludes the air gap and lets sound enter the part
Equal to that of air, which is exactly the gap the couplant must bridge
Equal to a vacuum, so it carries no sound at all across into the part
Lower than the part, so it blocks the sound from getting in at all
content.explanation: A couplant works mainly by excluding the air gap. Air has a very large impedance mismatch with the transducer and the part, so an air gap reflects almost all the sound; replacing it with a liquid or gel, even one whose impedance is below that of the metal, lets far more sound enter the part.
distractors: Air's impedance is the problem couplant solves, not what it provides.
A vacuum transmits no sound; couplant is a liquid or gel.
Couplant transmits sound rather than blocking it.

content.stem: The region of the beam just in front of the transducer with strong interference is the:
options: Near field (Fresnel zone)
Far field (Fraunhofer zone)
The backwall echo region
The couplant layer zone
content.explanation: The near field has pressure variations that make amplitude evaluation unreliable; beyond it, in the far field, the beam behaves more predictably.
distractors: The far field is beyond the near field, where the beam is more uniform.
The backwall is the far surface of the part, not a beam region.
The couplant layer is the coupling film, not a beam region.

content.stem: In the far field, the sound beam:
options: Spreads and weakens more predictably with distance
Fluctuates chaotically in both pressure and amplitude
Does not exist as any true beam region
Speeds the sound up as it travels further away
content.explanation: Beyond the near field the beam diverges and its amplitude falls in a predictable way, which is why evaluation is generally done in the far field.
distractors: Chaotic interference is characteristic of the near field.
The far field is where most evaluation occurs; it does exist.
Distance does not change the material's sound speed.

content.stem: Beam spread in the far field is reduced by:
options: Larger transducer diameter or higher frequency
Smaller transducer diameter or lower frequency
A thicker layer of couplant under the transducer
More receiver gain added in across the sweep
content.explanation: A larger element or higher frequency produces a more collimated beam with less divergence. Gain and couplant amount do not change beam spread.
distractors: Smaller diameter and lower frequency increase beam spread.
Couplant amount does not control beam spread.
Gain amplifies the signal; it does not change beam spread.

content.stem: A safety advantage of UT over radiography is that UT:
options: Uses sound and produces no ionizing radiation
Uses only a low, safe dose of ionizing radiation
Still needs film badges to be worn by the crew
Sets up a radiation area right around the work
content.explanation: UT uses mechanical sound waves and emits no ionizing radiation, so it avoids the radiation hazards and controls associated with radiography.
distractors: UT does not use ionizing radiation at all.
Film badges are a radiography control, not needed for UT sound.
UT does not create a radiation area.

content.stem: Which statement about UT fundamentals is correct?
options: UT sends sound into a part and uses echoes to find flaws and measure thickness
UT can only ever be used on thin sheet metal and never on any thicker section
UT needs no couplant at all and works fine straight through an open air gap
UT finds surface cracks only and can never measure the wall thickness
content.explanation: UT introduces sound, receives echoes from reflectors and the backwall, and uses timing and amplitude to find flaws and measure thickness in many materials.
distractors: UT works across a wide thickness range, not only thin sheet.
UT needs couplant; sound does not cross an air gap well.
Thickness measurement is a primary UT use.

content.stem: When sound crosses at an angle into a material of different velocity, it:
options: Refracts (bends)
Halts entirely
Changes color
Is all absorbed
content.explanation: A velocity change at an angled interface bends the sound beam, just as light refracts. This is the basis of angle-beam inspection.
distractors: The sound continues, refracted, rather than stopping.
Sound has no color to change.
Some energy transmits and refracts; it is not all lost.

content.stem: Snell's law relates the angles of incidence and refraction to the:
options: Sound velocities in the two materials
The densities of the two materials alone
The receiver gain set on the instrument
Diameter of the transducer crystal used
content.explanation: Snell's law states that the sine of the angle divided by the velocity is equal across the interface, so the refracted angle depends on the velocities.
distractors: Velocity, not density alone, governs the refracted angle in Snell's law.
Gain is an amplification setting, not part of the refraction relationship.
Transducer diameter affects beam spread, not the refracted angle.

content.stem: At normal (perpendicular) incidence, the beam:
options: Passes straight in without refraction or mode conversion
Bends sharply as it refracts on entry into the part
Splits into a shear wave through mode conversion at entry
Reflects fully back with none of it entering the part
content.explanation: When the beam strikes a surface perpendicularly, it does not bend and does not mode-convert; it travels straight in as the same mode.
distractors: There is no refraction at normal incidence.
Mode conversion requires an angle, not normal incidence.
Most of the sound transmits if impedances are similar; it does not all reflect.

content.stem: Mode conversion at an angled interface means:
options: Some energy changes between longitudinal and shear modes
The frequency of the beam doubles right at the interface
The couplant film changes into a thicker gel layer
The sound speeds up sharply as it crosses the interface
content.explanation: At an angle, part of the energy can convert from longitudinal to shear (or back), producing refracted waves of both modes at different angles.
distractors: Mode conversion does not double the frequency.
Mode conversion is a wave effect, not a couplant change.
Mode conversion changes wave mode, not the sound speed alone.

content.stem: Angle-beam inspection in steel typically uses a:
options: Refracted shear wave
A surface wave
A longitudinal wave
A radio wave
content.explanation: By choosing the wedge incidence so only the refracted shear wave remains, angle-beam setups inspect welds and similar geometries with shear waves.
distractors: Surface waves are a different mode used for surface flaws.
Above the first critical angle the refracted longitudinal wave is gone.
Radio waves are not ultrasonic.

content.stem: At the first critical angle, the refracted longitudinal wave:
options: Reaches 90 degrees, leaving only the refracted shear wave
Reaches 90 degrees and the shear wave disappears as well
Doubles in amplitude right as it enters the part metal
Turns into a surface wave running along the top face
content.explanation: At the first critical angle the longitudinal wave refracts to 90 degrees and no longer enters the part, so only the shear wave remains for angle-beam work.
distractors: The shear wave still remains beyond the first critical angle.
Amplitude does not double at the critical angle.
The surface wave appears at the second critical angle, not the first.

content.stem: At the second critical angle, the refracted shear wave reaches 90 degrees and a:
options: Surface wave is produced
A longitudinal wave forms
A backwall echo appears
A couplant film forms
content.explanation: At the second critical angle the shear wave refracts to 90 degrees along the surface, producing a surface (Rayleigh) wave.
distractors: The longitudinal wave is already gone above the first critical angle.
A backwall echo is a reflection, not a critical-angle effect.
The couplant film is the coupling layer, not a critical-angle product.

content.stem: Refracted-shear angle-beam inspection uses incidence angles:
options: Between the first and second critical angles
Below the first critical angle for any mode
Above the second critical angle in every case
At exactly zero degrees, straight into the part
content.explanation: Between the two critical angles only the shear wave exists in the part, which is the region used for shear angle-beam inspection.
distractors: Below the first critical angle both longitudinal and shear refract into the part.
Above the second critical angle the shear wave no longer enters the part.
Zero degrees is normal incidence, a straight-beam condition.

content.stem: At an interface, how much sound reflects versus transmits depends on the:
options: Acoustic impedance difference
The test frequency alone
The beam diameter alone
The pulse length alone
content.explanation: The greater the impedance mismatch, the more sound reflects and the less transmits. Similar impedances let most of the sound pass through.
distractors: Frequency does not by itself set the reflection and transmission at an interface.
Beam diameter affects coverage, not the reflection coefficient.
Pulse length affects resolution, not how much reflects at an interface.

content.stem: Longitudinal velocity in steel is commonly near:
options: About 0.23 in/microsecond (roughly 5900 m/s)
About 0.02 in/microsecond (roughly 510 m/s)
About 2.3 in/microsecond (roughly 58000 m/s)
Near 0 in/microsecond, since steel carries none
content.explanation: Longitudinal velocity in steel is roughly 0.23 inch per microsecond (about 5900 m/s). Use the correct value for the actual material and confirm against reference data.
distractors: 0.02 in/microsecond is far too low for steel.
2.3 in/microsecond is far too high for steel.
Velocity in steel is not zero.

content.stem: Using the wrong material velocity during setup will cause:
options: Incorrect distance and thickness readings
No change at all to the distance readings
A shift in the color of the display trace
A faster sweep speed set across the display
content.explanation: Distance and thickness are computed from velocity, so an incorrect velocity produces inaccurate readings even if the echoes look fine.
distractors: Velocity errors do affect the readings.
There is no color change involved.
Wrong velocity skews readings; it does not change sweep speed.

content.stem: A significant temperature change in the part generally:
options: Changes the sound velocity slightly and can affect readings
Has no effect at all on the velocity or on the readings taken
Shifts the color of the trace shown across the display screen
Reverses the direction that the sound beam travels in the part
content.explanation: Velocity varies with temperature, so large temperature differences between calibration and inspection can shift readings; corrections or on-part calibration may be needed.
distractors: Temperature does affect velocity and can affect readings.
Temperature is not about part color here.
Temperature does not reverse the beam.

content.stem: For a given material, attenuation generally:
options: Increases with higher frequency
Drops off with higher frequency
Is fixed regardless of frequency
Is set only by the receiver gain
content.explanation: Higher frequencies attenuate more, especially in coarse-grained material, which is one reason lower frequencies are used for thick or attenuative parts.
distractors: Attenuation rises, not falls, with higher frequency.
Attenuation does depend on frequency.
Gain amplifies the signal; it does not set the material attenuation.

content.stem: Scattering from grain structure can produce:
options: Noise (grass) on the display that can mask small echoes
A taller backwall echo standing well above the noise floor
A second backwall echo doubling up on the first one
A bright color band running right across the screen
content.explanation: Scattered sound shows as noise or grass on the A-scan, which can hide small flaw echoes, especially at higher frequencies in coarse material.
distractors: Scattering tends to weaken, not strengthen, the backwall.
Grain scatter raises noise; it does not double the backwall echo.
Scattering does not create a color band.

content.stem: Sound bending around the edge of a small reflector is called:
options: Diffraction
Refraction
Couplant flow
Gain rise
content.explanation: Diffraction is the spreading of sound around edges and small reflectors, an effect used in some advanced sizing but recognized at Level I as a wave behavior.
distractors: That bending around an edge is diffraction, not refraction.
Couplant flow is not a wave behavior term.
Gain is an instrument control, not a wave behavior.

content.stem: Beam divergence describes how the beam:
options: Spreads out with distance in the far field
Stays a perfect cylinder at every distance
Shifts in color as it travels further on
Turns right back on itself in the far field
content.explanation: Beyond the near field the beam diverges, lowering intensity and affecting how reflectors at the edges of the beam respond.
distractors: Real beams diverge; they are not perfect cylinders.
Divergence is not a color effect.
Divergence is spreading, not reversal.

content.stem: An angle-beam transducer uses a wedge to:
options: Introduce sound at an angle so it refracts to the desired angle in the part
Filter the beam down to one single chosen frequency before it enters
Damp the crystal so that the pulse is kept short on every shot
Focus the beam down to a tight point at a chosen depth in the part
content.explanation: The wedge sets the incidence angle so refraction and mode conversion produce the intended refracted shear angle in the material.
distractors: A wedge sets the entry angle; it is not a frequency filter.
Damping is done by the backing material, not the angle wedge.
The wedge sets the angle; focusing is done by a curved or lens element.

content.stem: The refracted angle in the part for a given wedge depends on the:
options: Velocities of the wedge and the part material
The gain and reject set on the instrument
The diameter of the transducer crystal
The pulse repetition rate of the instrument
content.explanation: Because refraction follows Snell's law, the refracted angle depends on the wedge and part velocities, so a wedge marked for steel gives a different angle in another material.
distractors: Gain and reject are amplitude settings; they do not change the refracted angle.
Transducer diameter affects beam spread, not the refracted angle.
Pulse repetition rate does not affect the refracted angle.

content.stem: Common refracted shear angles for weld inspection in steel are:
options: 45, 60, and 70 degrees
5, 10, and 15 degrees
0, 2, and 4 degrees
85, 87, and 89 degrees
content.explanation: Angle-beam weld inspection commonly uses 45, 60, and 70 degree refracted shear angles, selected for the geometry and expected flaw orientation.
distractors: 5 and 10 degrees are not typical refracted shear angles for welds.
0 degrees is straight beam, not angle beam.
85 and 89 degrees approach the surface-wave region, not typical weld angles.

content.stem: Couplant improves transmission into the part by:
options: Replacing the high-mismatch air gap with a better-matched liquid path
Pulling the air out from under the probe by means of a light suction
Shifting the test frequency to a value that suits the part better
Cooling the crystal so that the beam carries further into the part
content.explanation: By filling the air gap with a liquid or gel, the couplant reduces the severe impedance mismatch of air and lets far more sound enter the part.
distractors: Couplant fills the gap with liquid; it does not suck air out.
Couplant does not change the test frequency.
Couplant's role is coupling sound, not cooling.

content.stem: In the same material, longitudinal and shear waves have:
options: Different velocities
The same velocity
No velocity at all
Gain-set velocities
content.explanation: Each mode has its own velocity in a material, with shear slower than longitudinal, which must be accounted for when setting up shear angle-beam work.
distractors: The modes do not share the same velocity.
Both modes propagate; velocity is not zero.
Gain does not set wave velocity.

content.stem: For a highly attenuative casting, a reasonable choice is to:
options: Use a lower frequency to improve penetration
Use the very highest frequency available on hand
Scan it fully dry with no couplant applied at all
Turn the instrument right off between each pass
content.explanation: Lower frequencies scatter less and penetrate attenuative, coarse-grained material better, at some cost to resolution.
distractors: The highest frequency would attenuate badly in such material.
Couplant is still required for sound transmission.
Turning off the instrument does not inspect the part.

content.stem: An internal interface such as a lamination produces an echo because:
options: It presents an impedance change that reflects sound
It soaks up the entire beam so that none of it returns
It raises the local sound velocity at that depth
It amplifies the signal passing through that very spot
content.explanation: A lamination or similar internal boundary reflects sound due to the impedance change, returning an echo ahead of the backwall.
distractors: A lamination reflects sound; it does not absorb the entire beam.
A lamination is an interface that reflects sound; it does not raise the local velocity.
A lamination is a passive reflector; it does not amplify the signal.

content.stem: A reflector at the edge of the beam may give a:
options: Lower amplitude than the same reflector on the beam axis
Higher amplitude than the same reflector on the beam axis
A wider spread echo rather than any change in its height
A color change rather than any shift in the echo height
content.explanation: Sound intensity is lower toward the beam edges, so an off-axis reflector returns a weaker echo than it would on the beam centerline.
distractors: Off-axis reflectors usually give lower, not higher, amplitude.
Off-axis reflectors drop in amplitude; the echo is not simply wider.
There is no color change involved.

content.stem: A thickness gauge computes thickness from the echo time and the:
options: Material's sound velocity setting
The receiver gain setting in use
The pulse repetition rate set
The chosen test frequency value
content.explanation: Thickness equals half the round-trip time multiplied by the velocity, so the correct velocity must be set for the material.
distractors: Gain sets amplitude; it is not used in the thickness calculation.
Pulse repetition rate is how often pulses fire, not part of the thickness math.
Frequency affects resolution, not the time-to-thickness conversion.

content.stem: In immersion testing, the couplant is:
options: A water path between the transducer and the part
A thin dry film smeared across the transducer face
An air gap kept between the probe and the part face
A light oil floated on top of the water bath surface
content.explanation: Immersion testing uses a water column or bath to couple sound into the part, with the transducer not touching the surface.
distractors: Immersion uses water, not a dry film.
Air is the gap that coupling is meant to eliminate.
Immersion couples through the water itself, not an oil layer.

content.stem: In immersion testing, the water path has its own velocity, so the operator must account for the:
options: Time the sound spends in the water before entering the part
Nothing at all, since the water time can simply be left out
No calibration at all, since immersion removes the need for it
A doubling of the part reading brought on by the water path
content.explanation: Because sound travels through the water first, the water-path time is separated from the part signal during setup, often using a water-path or interface echo.
distractors: The water-path time is significant and must be separated, not ignored.
Immersion still requires calibration; water does not remove that need.
The water path is accounted for separately; it does not double the part reading.

content.stem: Surface waves are useful for detecting:
options: Surface and near-surface flaws that follow the contour
Deep internal voids buried far below the part surface
Flaws lying within the liquid bath around the part
Tight laminations lying flat deep inside the thick plate
content.explanation: Surface waves travel along the surface and can follow gentle contours, making them suitable for surface and near-surface flaws.
distractors: Deep internal voids are better found with bulk waves.
Surface waves travel on solids, not within liquids.
Surface waves suit surface flaws, not deep laminations.

content.stem: Shear angle beams are favored for many weld inspections because they:
options: Can reach the weld volume at an angle to detect typical weld flaws
Skim only the outer surface and never reach into the weld body itself
Need no calibration at all before the weld is scanned from each side
Read off the color of the weld cap rather than any returning echo
content.explanation: Angled shear waves can be directed into the weld and heat-affected zone to find cracks and fusion flaws that a straight beam might miss.
distractors: Shear angle beams travel through the volume, not only the surface.
Angle-beam work still requires calibration.
Ultrasound detects acoustic reflectors, not color.

content.stem: Mode-converted signals during angle-beam work can:
options: Produce extra indications the technician must recognize
Be safely ignored at will, since they carry no real meaning
Push the test frequency up as the angled beam travels on
Shift the color contrast right across the display screen
content.explanation: Mode conversion can create additional echoes that are not flaws, so the technician learns to recognize them rather than mistaking them for discontinuities.
distractors: They cannot simply be ignored; they must be recognized and understood.
Mode conversion adds indications; it does not change frequency.
It is unrelated to color contrast.

content.stem: The correct sound velocity for a material is obtained from:
options: Reference data or by calibrating on a known sample
The frequency printed on the transducer's own label
A single fixed value that suits every metal alike
The weight and the size of the part being tested
content.explanation: Velocities come from reference tables or from calibrating on a sample of known thickness and material, ensuring accurate readings.
distractors: The transducer label gives its frequency and size, not the part velocity.
Different materials have different velocities; one value does not fit all.
Weight and size do not give the sound velocity; reference data or calibration does.

content.stem: Which statement about wave behavior is correct?
options: Angled incidence causes refraction and mode conversion governed by the materials' velocities
Sound never bends at any interface at all, whatever the angle of incidence may be
Sound velocity is a single fixed value for every mode and every material alike
Test frequency has no real effect at all on either penetration or resolution
content.explanation: At an angle, sound refracts and can mode-convert according to Snell's law and the velocities involved, and frequency affects penetration and resolution.
distractors: Sound does bend (refract) at angled velocity changes.
Velocity varies by mode and material.
Frequency strongly affects penetration and resolution.

content.stem: A basic pulse-echo UT instrument includes a:
options: Pulser, receiver, and display
A transducer, a couplant, and a cable
A wedge, a reference block, and a gate
A battery, a keypad, and a carry case
content.explanation: The pulser drives the transducer, the receiver amplifies the returning echoes, and the display shows them, commonly as an A-scan.
distractors: Those are probe and coupling accessories, not instrument sections.
Those are calibration accessories and a feature, not core sections.
Those are physical fittings, not the functional sections.

content.stem: The pulser in a UT instrument:
options: Sends an electrical pulse that drives the transducer
Cools the probe element down once each scan pass is done
Sets the display brightness before the scanning starts
Measures the surface color across the test part
content.explanation: The pulser delivers a short, high-voltage electrical pulse to the transducer, which converts it into a sound pulse.
distractors: The pulser drives the transducer; it does not cool the probe.
The pulser excites the transducer; it does not set brightness.
The pulser does not measure color.

content.stem: The receiver in a UT instrument:
options: Amplifies and processes the returning echo signals
Fires the electrical pulse that drives the crystal
Sets the sound velocity used inside the test part
Spreads the couplant film across the test surface
content.explanation: The receiver amplifies the small voltages the transducer produces from echoes and conditions them for display.
distractors: Generating the transmit pulse is the pulser's job, not the receiver's.
Material velocity is a property of the part, not set by the receiver.
Couplant is applied manually; the receiver does not provide it.

content.stem: A UT transducer converts:
options: Electrical energy to sound and sound back to electrical energy
Electrical energy to light and light back to electrical energy
Heat energy straight into sound and sound back into heat again
Surface pressure straight into a reading shown on a dial gauge
content.explanation: The transducer changes electrical pulses into sound and converts returning sound echoes back into electrical signals, working in both directions.
distractors: The transducer works with sound and electricity, not light.
A UT transducer converts electrical energy and sound, not heat.
It converts electrical energy and sound, not pressure to a dial.

content.stem: The element in a UT transducer works by the:
options: Piezoelectric effect
Photoelectric effect
Thermoelectric effect
A chemical reaction
content.explanation: A piezoelectric element changes shape when voltage is applied (making sound) and generates voltage when sound deforms it (receiving echoes).
distractors: The photoelectric effect involves light and electrons, not UT elements.
The element is piezoelectric, not thermoelectric.
It is a physical effect, not a chemical reaction.

content.stem: Common piezoelectric element materials include:
options: Ceramics such as lead zirconate titanate and composites
Thin aluminum foil pressed against the metal wear plate
Plain window glass cut down to the right thickness
Soft rubber moulded to fit inside the probe housing
content.explanation: Modern elements are often ceramics such as PZT or piezocomposites; quartz and lithium niobate are also used. Foil, glass, and rubber are not piezoelectric elements.
distractors: Aluminum foil is not a piezoelectric element.
Plain glass is not used as the active element.
Rubber is not a piezoelectric element.

content.stem: The fundamental frequency of a transducer element is set mainly by its:
options: Thickness
Diameter
Backing mass
Wear face
content.explanation: A thinner element resonates at a higher frequency. Element thickness is the primary factor setting the transducer's frequency.
distractors: Diameter affects beam spread and near-field length, not the fundamental frequency.
The backing controls damping and bandwidth, not the fundamental frequency.
The wear face protects the element; it does not set the frequency.

content.stem: The backing (damping) material behind the element:
options: Controls ringing and shortens the pulse for better resolution
Stretches the ringing out and lengthens the pulse on each shot
Sets the fundamental frequency that the element rings at
Couples the sound across the gap into the test part itself
content.explanation: Damping shortens the pulse by absorbing element vibration, improving near-surface resolution at some cost to sensitivity.
distractors: Damping reduces ringing and shortens the pulse, the opposite of lengthening it.
Fundamental frequency is set by element thickness, not the backing.
Coupling into the part is the couplant's role, not the backing's.

content.stem: Heavier damping generally gives:
options: A shorter pulse and better resolution but lower sensitivity
A longer pulse and higher sensitivity but a poorer resolution
No change at all to either the pulse length or the sensitivity
A much wider beam spread set up around the probe on every shot
content.explanation: More damping shortens the pulse, improving resolution and reducing the dead zone, while reducing peak sensitivity. The design balances the two.
distractors: Heavier damping shortens, not lengthens, the pulse.
Damping does change pulse length and sensitivity.
Damping shortens the pulse; it does not widen the beam.

content.stem: A contact transducer is used by:
options: Placing it on the part with a thin couplant film
Submerging the entire part down in a tank of water
Holding it up in the air a short way off the part
Bonding it permanently onto the test part surface
content.explanation: Contact transducers are coupled directly to the part surface with a thin couplant layer for routine hand scanning.
distractors: Submerging the part describes immersion testing.
Holding it in air leaves a sound-blocking air gap.
Contact transducers are not permanently bonded for routine testing.

content.stem: A dual-element (transmit-receive) transducer is well suited to:
options: Thin material, near-surface, and corrosion thickness measurement
Thick heavy forgings carrying deeply buried internal flaws only
Long-range guided-wave testing along the length of a long pipe
Steering the beam round to a chosen refracted angle inside the part
content.explanation: Dual-element probes use separate transmit and receive elements, reducing the dead zone and improving near-surface and thin-wall or corrosion thickness measurement.
distractors: Dual elements are favored for thin and near-surface work, not only thick forgings.
Dual-element probes suit thin near-surface work, not long-range pipe runs.
A dual-element straight probe does not steer the beam to an angle.

content.stem: A dual-element transducer reduces the:
options: Near-surface dead zone
The need to calibrate
The sound velocity
All beam spread
content.explanation: By separating transmit and receive, the dual probe lessens the dead zone right under the surface, helping measure thin walls and detect near-surface flaws.
distractors: Dual-element probes still require calibration.
Velocity is a property of the part, not reduced by the probe.
Beam spread is not eliminated by using a dual element.

content.stem: An angle-beam transducer is a straight element mounted on a:
options: Wedge that refracts the sound to an angle in the part
Delay line that holds the element up off the surface
Curved shoe contoured to match the part surface well
Protective membrane stretched across the element face
content.explanation: An angle-beam assembly couples a transducer to an angled wedge so the refracted beam enters the part at the intended angle.
distractors: An angle-beam probe uses an angled wedge, not a flat delay line.
A contoured shoe is for curved contact, not for angling the beam.
A wear membrane protects the face; it does not refract the beam.

content.stem: Immersion transducers are designed to operate:
options: With a water path between probe and part
Pressed firmly down onto the part surface
Across a vacuum gap up to the part
With no coupling medium present at all
content.explanation: Immersion probes work through a water column or bath rather than direct contact, often allowing focused beams and automated scanning.
distractors: Pressed-on use describes contact probes.
Sound cannot couple through a vacuum.
A coupling medium (water) is required.

content.stem: A focused immersion transducer is used to:
options: Concentrate the beam for better sensitivity and resolution at a depth
Widen the beam right out so that it covers far more area per pass
Slow the sound right down as it travels along the water path to the part
Heat the water in the tank up to speed the sound along
content.explanation: Focusing concentrates sound at a chosen depth, improving sensitivity and resolution there, commonly in immersion setups.
distractors: Focusing narrows, not widens, the beam.
A focused probe shapes the beam; it does not slow the sound.
Focusing is about the beam, not heating the water.

content.stem: A delay-line transducer places a short standoff in front of the element to:
options: Move the initial pulse away for better near-surface resolution
Slow the entire sweep speed right down across the display screen
Change the measured thickness of the actual part being tested
Color the returning echo so that it stands out on the screen
content.explanation: The delay line introduces a known short path so the entry signal is separated from near-surface echoes, helping thin-material and near-surface work, and protecting the element on hot surfaces.
distractors: A delay line shifts the initial pulse; it does not slow the sweep.
It does not change the part thickness.
It does not color the echo.

content.stem: A contact transducer often has a wear face (wear plate) to:
options: Protect the element from abrasion and damage
Set the refracted angle of the beam in the part
Raise the operating frequency of the element
Replace the need for couplant on the surface
content.explanation: The wear face protects the element during scanning on rough surfaces and can aid coupling. It is inspected and replaced as it wears.
distractors: The refracted angle is set by a wedge, not the wear face.
The wear face does not change the transducer frequency.
Couplant is still required; the wear face does not replace it.

content.stem: UT transducer cables and connectors should be:
options: In good condition, since damage can disrupt the signal
Allowed to fray, as worn cores still carry the signal
Loosely connected, since the contact makes no difference
Left damp inside, since the moisture helps the signal along
content.explanation: Damaged cables and connectors can cause signal loss or noise, so they are kept in good condition and the correct type is used.
distractors: Fraying is damage that degrades the signal.
Bad connections do affect the signal.
Moisture inside connectors causes problems, not a benefit.

content.stem: Selecting a higher transducer frequency tends to favor:
options: Resolution and small-flaw sensitivity on fine-grained, thinner parts
Penetration through thick coarse castings that strongly attenuate sound
The lowest equipment cost rather than any real technical gain at all
No real difference at all to the detection on any kind of part
content.explanation: Higher frequency improves resolution and small-flaw detection but penetrates less, so it suits finer-grained, thinner sections; thick attenuative parts favor lower frequency.
distractors: Thick castings usually need lower frequency for penetration.
Frequency choice is a technical decision, not just cost.
Frequency has clear technical effects.

content.stem: A larger-diameter transducer generally provides:
options: A more collimated beam and greater coverage per pass
A more rapidly diverging beam at each test depth
No real change at all to the shape of the sound beam
A much shorter pulse length set on each shot
content.explanation: Larger elements give a more directional beam with less far-field spread and cover more area, though small elements can be handier on small or curved parts.
distractors: Larger elements diverge less, not more.
Element size does affect the beam.
Element size affects beam spread, not pulse length.

content.stem: A broadband (highly damped) transducer tends to have:
options: A short pulse and good resolution
Long ringing and narrow bandwidth
No real frequency content at all
More sensitivity but less resolution
content.explanation: Broadband probes produce short pulses with good axial resolution; narrowband probes ring longer with higher sensitivity at a specific frequency.
distractors: Long ringing is a narrowband characteristic.
A transducer does have frequency content.
Broadband damping gives a short pulse with lower, not higher, sensitivity.

content.stem: Choosing a transducer involves matching the:
options: Frequency, size, and type to the part and the flaws sought
The element size to the size of the instrument display
The gain setting to the instrument's printed serial number
The pulse repetition rate to the type of couplant being used
content.explanation: Frequency, element size, and probe type (contact, dual, angle, immersion) are selected for the material, thickness, geometry, and expected flaws.
distractors: Element size is chosen for the inspection, not matched to the screen size.
Gain is set during calibration, not matched to a serial number.
Pulse repetition rate is not matched to the couplant when choosing a probe.

content.stem: Portable UT flaw detectors are typically:
options: Battery-capable handheld instruments with an A-scan display
Bench-only mains units that never run on a battery at all
Large fixed consoles that need a full two people to carry them
Rack-mounted laboratory units that run only from the mains power
content.explanation: Field UT detectors are portable, often battery-powered, with an A-scan display and the controls needed for calibration and inspection.
distractors: Portable detectors are handheld and battery-capable.
Portable detectors are light handheld units.
Portable detectors are handheld and battery-capable, not rack units.

content.stem: To protect transducers, the technician should:
options: Avoid dropping them and check the face for wear and cracks
Drag them hard across the rough surface to save scanning time
Store them permanently soaking down in a tank of water
Tap them firmly on the steel bench to seat the element
content.explanation: Transducers are fragile; dropping or rough handling can crack the element or wear face, so they are handled carefully and inspected.
distractors: Dragging hard without care damages the wear face and element.
Permanent water storage is not how contact probes are kept.
Striking a transducer can damage it.

content.stem: Dual-element probes are often built with a slight roof angle so the transmit and receive beams:
options: Cross at a focal depth for best response there
Cancel each other out at the focal depth below
Run parallel and never meet within the part
Reflect off the wear face without entering at all
content.explanation: The crossed beams of a dual probe give a pseudo-focus at a depth, optimizing response for thin walls or a target thickness range.
distractors: The crossed beams reinforce response at a focal depth; they do not cancel.
The roof angle makes the beams cross, not run parallel without meeting.
The beams enter the part; they do not merely reflect off the wear face.

content.stem: For hot surfaces, special considerations include using:
options: High-temperature probes or delay lines and limiting contact time
Any standard contact probe held on for as long as the scan takes
No couplant at all, since the heat itself carries the sound across
Ordinary room-temperature couplant simply applied a little thicker
content.explanation: High-temperature probes, delay lines, suitable couplants, and limited dwell protect the transducer and keep readings valid on hot parts.
distractors: Standard probes can be damaged by heat without precautions.
A suitable high-temperature couplant is still needed.
Hot surfaces need high-temperature couplant, not ordinary couplant.

content.stem: The receiver protects its input from the strong pulser voltage so that:
options: The instrument can transmit and then receive small echoes
The screen can refresh its entire display in between each shot
The battery can recharge itself fully in between each shot
The couplant film can dry off between each of the scan passes
content.explanation: Protection lets the same circuitry handle the large transmit pulse and then amplify the tiny returning echoes without damage.
distractors: The protection circuit guards the receiver input; it is not for refresh.
The circuit protects the receiver; it does not recharge the battery.
It is unrelated to couplant drying.

content.stem: Common UT transducer connectors include:
options: BNC, Lemo, and microdot types
Standard household wall plugs
Plain garden hose fittings
Optical-fiber light connectors
content.explanation: UT probes use connectors such as BNC, Lemo, and microdot. Using the correct mating connector and a good cable preserves signal quality.
distractors: Household plugs are not UT transducer connectors.
Garden hose fittings are not signal connectors.
Conventional UT uses electrical, not optical-fiber, connectors.

content.stem: Typical UT instrument controls include:
options: Gain, range, delay, and reject
Brightness and the contrast
Frequency and the velocity
Probe angle and the wedge type
content.explanation: UT controls set gain (sensitivity), range and delay (sweep), and reject, among others. Aperture, developer time, and amperage belong to other methods.
distractors: Those are display adjustments, not the core UT controls.
Frequency and velocity are setup values, not the control group.
Angle and wedge are probe choices, not instrument controls.

content.stem: A transducer is usually marked with its:
options: Nominal frequency and size
The material velocity value
The acceptance criteria
The scanning gain setting
content.explanation: Probes are labeled with nominal frequency and element size (and type), which the technician records and matches to the procedure.
distractors: Material velocities are looked up or calibrated, not marked on the probe.
Acceptance criteria come from the specification, not the probe marking.
Scanning gain is set during calibration, not marked on the probe.

content.stem: The same piezoelectric element can transmit and receive because it:
options: Converts voltage to motion and motion back to voltage
Converts voltage to motion but never the other way round
Stores the returning echoes chemically until read
Turns voltage to light and the light back to voltage
content.explanation: The piezoelectric effect is reversible, so one element both produces sound from voltage and produces voltage from received sound.
distractors: The piezoelectric effect is reversible, so it also converts motion back to voltage.
The element does not store echoes chemically; it converts them to voltage directly.
The element works with sound and voltage, not light.

content.stem: For a small-diameter pipe, a useful accessory is a:
options: Curved shoe or contoured wedge matching the surface
A flat shoe pressed straight onto the tight pipe curve
A thick rubber pad laid over the tight pipe curve
A heavy clamp gripping right around the small pipe
content.explanation: A contoured shoe or wedge matches the curved surface for proper coupling and beam entry; a flat shoe couples poorly on a tight curve.
distractors: A flat shoe on a tight curve couples poorly.
A contoured shoe matches the curve; a flat pad couples poorly.
Coupling on small pipe needs a contoured shoe, not a clamp.

content.stem: Before inspection, the technician confirms the instrument and probe are:
options: Functioning and set up per the procedure
Assumed good without any actual check first
Left fully disconnected from the instrument
Submerged deep in a full tub of couplant
content.explanation: A functional check and procedure-based setup confirm the instrument, cable, and probe work before calibration and inspection.
distractors: Equipment is verified, not assumed good.
A disconnected probe cannot inspect.
Submerging a contact probe in couplant is not the setup.

content.stem: A cracked transducer element may show as:
options: Weak or erratic signals and poor calibration
A shift in the color of the screen trace shown
A sudden jump in the measured part thickness
A change in the measured weight of the test part
content.explanation: Element damage often causes low or unstable response and difficulty calibrating, signaling the probe should be checked or replaced.
distractors: Element damage is not a color effect.
A cracked element gives weak erratic signals, not a thickness jump.
Part weight is unrelated to a damaged element.

content.stem: With equipment, the Level I technician is generally expected to:
options: Operate it and perform routine checks under direction
Design new transducers to suit the inspection job
Set the calibration intervals used for the entire site
Write the inspection procedures for the other hands
content.explanation: A Level I operates the instrument and probes and performs routine checks, recording results; design and procedure approval are higher-level functions.
distractors: Designing transducers is not a Level I function.
Setting calibration intervals is above the Level I.
Writing procedures is above the Level I scope.

content.stem: Which statement about UT equipment is correct?
options: A pulser-receiver drives a piezoelectric transducer chosen by frequency, size, and type for the job
A single universal probe suits every inspection job, whatever the part or the flaw being sought
A UT transducer must always touch the part directly and can never work through any water immersion path
Worn and damaged cables make no difference at all to the quality of the returned signal
content.explanation: The instrument pulses and receives through a piezoelectric transducer selected for the application, and good cables and care keep the signal reliable.
distractors: Different probes suit different jobs; there is no single universal probe.
UT also works through a water path in immersion testing.
Damaged cables can degrade the signal.

content.stem: On an A-scan display, the horizontal and vertical axes represent:
options: Time or distance horizontally, amplitude vertically
Amplitude horizontally and surface color vertically
Part temperature horizontally and weight vertically
Gain horizontally and the couplant film vertically
content.explanation: The A-scan shows travel time (proportional to distance) along the horizontal axis and echo amplitude along the vertical axis.
distractors: The axes are distance/time and amplitude, not amplitude and color.
The A-scan does not display temperature or weight.
Gain and couplant are settings, not the A-scan axes.

content.stem: The signal at the left of the A-scan from the sound entering the part is the:
options: Initial pulse (main bang)
A far backwall echo signal
An interior flaw echo
The reject control
content.explanation: The initial pulse marks the start of the sound entering the part; reflectors and the backwall appear to its right based on their depth.
distractors: The backwall echo appears at the far surface position, not at the start.
A flaw echo appears between the initial pulse and backwall.
Reject is a control, not a displayed echo.

content.stem: The backwall echo appears on the sweep at a horizontal position corresponding to:
options: The full thickness of the part
The entry surface zero start point
Half of the part thickness
The near-field length only
content.explanation: After calibration, the backwall echo sits at the screen position matching the part thickness, with flaw echoes appearing at shallower positions.
distractors: The entry surface is the zero position; the backwall is at full thickness.
The backwall corresponds to full thickness, not half.
The near-field length is a beam property, not the backwall position.

content.stem: A flaw echo between the initial pulse and the backwall indicates a reflector:
options: At a depth between the surface and the back surface
Right at the entry surface of the part under test
From a stray signal running along the probe cable
From a mark sitting on the glass of the display screen
content.explanation: Its horizontal position gives the reflector's depth; an echo before the backwall corresponds to a reflector within the thickness.
distractors: An interior flaw echo corresponds to a reflector within the part.
Cable signals are not depth-positioned flaw echoes.
The echo represents a reflector in the part, not a mark on the glass.

content.stem: Echo height is often expressed as a percentage of:
options: Full screen height (FSH)
The width of the echo trace
The full sweep range
The pulse repeat rate
content.explanation: Amplitude is read as a percent of full screen height, used for reference levels and recording thresholds.
distractors: Amplitude is referenced to screen height, not the echo's width.
The sweep range is a distance setting, not the amplitude reference.
Pulse repetition rate is unrelated to expressing echo height.

content.stem: The gain control adjusts:
options: The amplification of the signal, in decibels
The measured thickness of the entire test part
The sound velocity set for the test part
The type of couplant used on the surface
content.explanation: Gain raises or lowers signal amplitude, usually in decibels, to set sensitivity and bring echoes to reference height.
distractors: Gain does not change the part thickness.
Gain does not change the material velocity.
Gain does not change the couplant type.

content.stem: An increase of about 6 dB corresponds to roughly:
options: Doubling the signal amplitude
Halving the signal amplitude
No change at all to amplitude
A tenfold rise in the amplitude
content.explanation: About 6 dB is roughly a factor of two in amplitude, and about 20 dB is roughly a factor of ten. These relationships help set reference levels.
distractors: 6 dB up doubles, not halves, the amplitude.
6 dB is a change, not zero effect.
About 20 dB, not 6 dB, is a tenfold change.

content.stem: The range (sweep) control sets:
options: The depth or sound-path span shown across the screen
The flow of couplant held under the moving probe head
The operating frequency of the transducer in use
The surface hardness of the part that is tested
content.explanation: Range determines how much material depth or sound path the screen width represents, chosen to display the region of interest.
distractors: Range does not control couplant flow.
Range does not change the transducer frequency.
Range does not affect part hardness.

content.stem: The delay (zero offset) control:
options: Shifts the displayed start so the correct zero point is shown
Raises the amplification so the weaker echoes show up on screen
Changes the sound velocity used right through the test part
Adds more couplant film in under the moving probe face
content.explanation: Delay positions the sweep so the entry surface reads as zero, correcting for wedge or delay-line and cable timing.
distractors: Delay does not change gain.
Delay does not change the material velocity.
Delay does not add couplant.

content.stem: The reject (suppression) control removes low-level signals but should be used cautiously because it can:
options: Be nonlinear and hide small relevant echoes
Always improve the accuracy of every reading
Boost the penetration deep into the part
Shift the set material velocity value
content.explanation: Reject can suppress noise but may be nonlinear and remove small real echoes, so many procedures limit or prohibit its use. The technician follows the procedure.
distractors: Reject does not always improve accuracy and can hide echoes.
Reject does not increase penetration.
Reject does not change the material velocity.

content.stem: The dead zone is the region:
options: Just below the surface where echoes are masked by the initial pulse
Just ahead of the backwall where the echoes merge into the back echo
Just outside the part where the beam spreads out into the air
Within the probe cable where the stray signals pile up
content.explanation: Right after the initial pulse, near-surface echoes can be hidden, creating a dead zone. Dual-element or delay-line probes reduce it.
distractors: The dead zone is near the entry surface, not the backwall.
The dead zone is within the near-surface material, not outside the part.
The dead zone is an acoustic effect, not a cable region.

content.stem: Common contact couplants include:
options: Water, oil, glycerin, grease, and gels
Acetone or other quick-drying solvents
A thin layer of trapped air gap
A dry paper shim under the probe
content.explanation: Liquids and gels such as water, oil, glycerin, grease, and commercial gels couple sound into the part. Dry powder, air, and sand do not couple effectively.
distractors: Volatile solvents flash off and do not couple sound.
Air is the gap couplant is meant to remove.
A dry shim blocks coupling; couplants wet the surface.

content.stem: Couplant is selected considering surface condition, temperature, position, and:
options: Removability and compatibility with the part
The transducer's own printed serial number label
The battery charge left in the instrument
The sweep range set across the display
content.explanation: Couplant choice weighs viscosity for the surface and orientation, temperature rating, ease of removal, and not harming the part (for example corrosion or residue concerns).
distractors: The transducer serial number does not affect couplant choice.
Battery level does not drive couplant selection.
The sweep range is a display setting, not a couplant consideration.

content.stem: To keep readings valid, the couplant and its application should be:
options: Consistent between calibration and inspection
Changed at random all through the inspection
Different for each single reading that is taken
Left off entirely while contact testing
content.explanation: Large changes in couplant or coupling pressure can shift amplitude, so calibration and inspection use consistent coupling.
distractors: Random changes can shift amplitude and readings.
Differing coupling each reading reduces repeatability.
Some couplant is required for contact UT.

content.stem: Too little couplant typically causes:
options: Weak or lost signals from poor coupling
Greater penetration deep into the part
A stronger, cleaner signal on the screen
A shift in the set material velocity
content.explanation: Inadequate couplant lets air interfere, weakening or losing the signal. Adequate, consistent couplant maintains coupling.
distractors: Poor coupling reduces, not increases, penetration of the signal.
Too little couplant weakens the signal, not strengthens it.
Couplant amount does not change material velocity.

content.stem: The scanning surface should be:
options: Clean and smooth enough for good coupling and beam entry
Left heavy with scale and oil so the probe just slides along
Roughened with coarse deep grinding marks across it
Of any condition at all, since it has no real effect
content.explanation: Loose scale, heavy paint, dirt, or roughness can block coupling and scatter the beam, so the surface is prepared as the procedure requires.
distractors: Heavy scale and oil interfere with coupling.
A rough surface scatters the beam and harms coupling.
Surface condition does affect results.

content.stem: After distance calibration, a reflector's depth is read from:
options: Its horizontal position on the sweep
Its color shown on the display screen
The amount of couplant being applied
The receiver gain currently set
content.explanation: The horizontal position corresponds to sound path or depth once the sweep is calibrated, letting the technician locate the reflector.
distractors: Echoes are not color-coded for depth.
Couplant does not set the depth reading.
Gain sets amplitude, not horizontal depth position.

content.stem: Echo amplitude is used as a reference but by itself is:
options: Not a direct measure of flaw size
An exact readout of the flaw size
Set by the part thickness alone
Free of any flaw orientation effect
content.explanation: Amplitude depends on size, orientation, depth, and other factors, so it is compared against references rather than read as an exact size, with sizing being a higher-level task.
distractors: Amplitude depends on many factors and is not an exact flaw size.
Amplitude is not simply proportional to part thickness.
Amplitude strongly depends on reflector orientation, not independent of it.

content.stem: Bringing a reference reflector echo to a set screen height establishes the:
options: Reference sensitivity level for the inspection
The sound velocity used through the test part
The horizontal sweep range set on the screen
The pulse repetition rate set on the instrument
content.explanation: Adjusting gain so a reference reflector reaches a defined height sets the sensitivity from which scanning and recording levels are referenced.
distractors: Velocity is set during distance calibration, not by this sensitivity step.
Sweep range is a distance setting, not the sensitivity reference.
Pulse repetition rate is unrelated to setting the reference sensitivity.

content.stem: Besides the A-scan, other UT presentations include:
options: B-scan and C-scan views
RF and video display modes
Time-of-flight readout only
Frequency spectrum plots
content.explanation: B-scan shows a cross-sectional view and C-scan a plan view of an area; the A-scan remains the basic waveform display for conventional UT.
distractors: RF and video are A-scan modes, not separate presentations.
A numeric readout is not an imaging presentation.
A spectrum plot is signal analysis, not a scan presentation.

content.stem: Raising gain too high can:
options: Lift noise and grass that obscure real echoes
Sharpen and clarify each real echo on screen
Raise the sound velocity right through the part
Add fresh couplant in under the probe face
content.explanation: Excess gain raises background noise along with signals, which can mask relevant echoes, so sensitivity is set to the procedure level.
distractors: Too much gain can obscure rather than clarify echoes.
Gain does not change velocity.
Gain does not add couplant.

content.stem: The initial pulse on the screen should not be mistaken for:
options: A flaw indication
A control setting
The couplant film
A stray cable signal
content.explanation: The initial pulse is the entry signal, not a reflector in the part, so the technician distinguishes it from genuine flaw echoes.
distractors: The initial pulse is not a setting on the screen.
The initial pulse is not the couplant.
The initial pulse is not the cable.

content.stem: On a thin part, several evenly spaced echoes across the screen are usually:
options: Multiple backwall reflections
A row of separate small flaws
Repeated couplant echoes
Stray cable reflections
content.explanation: Repeated backwall echoes appear at equal spacing as the sound bounces between surfaces; recognizing them avoids mistaking them for flaws.
distractors: Evenly spaced repeats are backwall multiples, not separate flaws.
They are part backwall reflections, not couplant echoes.
They are not cable reflections.

content.stem: On a hot surface, the couplant must be:
options: Rated for the temperature so it does not break down or boil off
Plain tap water poured on, which flashes off the hot metal
Left off entirely, since the surface heat carries the sound by itself
Frozen solid first, then pressed down onto the hot surface
content.explanation: High-temperature couplants are used on hot parts so coupling is maintained without flashing off, and contact time is limited to protect the probe.
distractors: Plain water can flash off on hot surfaces.
Some couplant is required; it cannot be omitted.
A frozen couplant would not couple properly.

content.stem: The displayed depth scale is correct only when the instrument is set to the:
options: Correct material velocity and calibrated
The maximum gain across the entire sweep
The highest pulse repetition rate set
A wide sweep range set on the screen
