content.explanation: Depth and thickness readings depend on a correct velocity and a valid calibration; otherwise positions and thicknesses are wrong.
distractors: Maximum gain does not make the depth scale correct.
Pulse repetition rate does not set the depth-scale accuracy.
Sweep range sets what is shown, not the depth-scale accuracy by itself.

content.stem: Whether reject may be used is determined by:
options: The written procedure or specification
How fast the scan has to be run on site
The chosen transducer frequency
The battery charge in the unit
content.explanation: Because reject can affect linearity, its use (if any) is governed by the procedure, and the technician follows that requirement.
distractors: Speed does not justify using reject where the procedure restricts it.
Transducer frequency does not determine whether reject is allowed.
Battery level does not govern reject use.

content.stem: Reading the A-scan, the Level I technician:
options: Recognizes and records echoes and their positions
Sets the final accept and reject criteria for that job
Approves the inspection procedures used on site
Sizes each flaw to code from the echo heights
content.explanation: A Level I identifies and records echoes, positions, and amplitudes; evaluating and sizing to acceptance criteria is a higher-level task.
distractors: Acceptance criteria are set above the Level I.
Approving procedures is a Level III function.
Flaw sizing to code is a Level II responsibility.

content.stem: After inspection, couplant is generally:
options: Removed as required to leave the part in acceptable condition
Left thick on the part metal to seal it against any corrosion
Left as a thin film so the probe keeps gliding easily next time
Baked onto the surface so that it stays put for next time
content.explanation: Residual couplant is cleaned off as the procedure requires so it does not cause corrosion or interfere with later steps.
distractors: Leaving thick couplant can cause corrosion or interfere later.
Couplant is cleaned off as required, not left on as a glide film.
Couplant is removed, not baked on.

content.stem: So that screen readings are trustworthy, instruments are periodically checked for:
options: Vertical (amplitude) and horizontal (distance) linearity
The clock and the date setting on the instrument display
The viscosity of the couplant gel that is applied
The cosmetic finish of the instrument's outer casing
content.explanation: Linearity checks confirm the display responds proportionally in amplitude and accurately in distance, supporting valid readings. The Level I performs such checks under direction.
distractors: The clock setting is not a performance characteristic that is checked.
Couplant viscosity is a couplant property, not an instrument linearity check.
Cosmetic finish is not a performance characteristic that is checked.

content.stem: When echoes are referenced to a set height, the technician records the:
options: Gain or dB used and the reference level
Just the time of day on the clock
The probe's original purchase order date
The ambient room noise in the area
content.explanation: Recording the gain and reference level lets the inspection be repeated and compared, supporting traceability.
distractors: The time of day alone does not capture the sensitivity setup.
The probe's purchase date is not the needed record.
Ambient acoustic noise is not what is recorded for the reference setup.

content.stem: To read the display reliably, the technician should view it:
options: With adequate, glare-free lighting on the screen
Under bright direct sunlight falling on the screen
From right across the room away from the unit
With the screen switched right off
content.explanation: A clear, glare-free view of the screen helps the technician see small echoes and read positions accurately.
distractors: Glaring sunlight washes out the display.
Across the room is too far to read fine detail.
The screen must be on to be read.

content.stem: Which statement about the display and couplant is correct?
options: The A-scan shows distance horizontally and amplitude vertically, and consistent couplant keeps readings valid
The A-scan reads the flaw depth from the trace color, and the couplant choice has no real effect on the readings
Reject can be turned right up quite safely, since it never hides any of the small relevant echoes
Contact UT needs no couplant, since sound crosses the dry air gap into the part by itself just fine
content.explanation: The A-scan plots distance against amplitude, gain sets sensitivity, reject is used cautiously, and consistent couplant maintains valid readings.
distractors: Depth is read from horizontal position, not color.
Reject can hide small echoes and is used cautiously.
Couplant is required for contact UT.

content.stem: Calibration before UT is done to:
options: Set distance and sensitivity so readings are accurate and repeatable
Warm the part through so the sound travels into it more easily
Clean the entire scanning surface right down before any readings are taken
Color the display trace so that the echoes stand out more clearly
content.explanation: Calibration establishes the distance (sweep) scale and the sensitivity reference so depths and amplitudes are accurate and the inspection is repeatable.
distractors: Calibration sets distance and sensitivity; it does not heat the part.
Surface cleaning is prep, not what calibration achieves.
Calibration does not color the display.

content.stem: Two main aspects of UT calibration are:
options: Distance (sweep) and sensitivity (amplitude reference)
The surface color and the weight of the part being tested
The couplant gel and the probe cable that are in use
The receiver gain by itself with nothing else set
content.explanation: Distance calibration sets the horizontal scale; sensitivity calibration sets the reference amplitude. Both are needed for valid results.
distractors: Color and weight are not calibration aspects.
Couplant and cable are equipment items, not the two calibration aspects.
Gain alone is only part of sensitivity setup.

content.stem: The IIW block is commonly used to:
options: Calibrate distance and check angle-beam index and angle
Measure the surface hardness of the test part metal
Store the spare probes and the cables out on the job
Set the pulse repetition rate used on the instrument
content.explanation: The IIW (International Institute of Welding) block supports distance calibration, beam index point location, refracted angle verification, and resolution checks.
distractors: Hardness is measured with a hardness tester, not an IIW block.
The IIW block is a calibration reference, not a storage case.
Pulse repetition rate is an instrument setting, not an IIW block function.

content.stem: A step wedge or step block is used to:
options: Calibrate or verify thickness readings at known thicknesses
Verify the refracted angle of an angle-beam probe used in steel
Measure the beam spread of the probe out in the far field
Set the reject level needed to clear the baseline grass
content.explanation: A step block provides known thicknesses to calibrate or verify a thickness gauge or sweep across a range.
distractors: Refracted angle is verified on an angle block, not a step block.
Beam spread is not what a step block measures.
The reject level is an instrument setting, not a step-block function.

content.stem: A flat-bottom hole (FBH) in a reference block serves as a:
options: Known reflector for setting sensitivity
A standard depth marker stamped in the block
A couplant reservoir for the probe
A mounting point for the angle-beam wedge
content.explanation: Flat-bottom holes are machined reference reflectors of known size and depth used to set and compare sensitivity.
distractors: An FBH is a reflector for sensitivity, not a depth marker.
It is not a couplant reservoir.
An FBH is a reflector, not a wedge mount.

content.stem: A side-drilled hole (SDH) is often used as a reference reflector for:
options: Angle-beam distance-amplitude and sensitivity setup
Couplant performance checks over the entire test surface
Surface roughness checks over the part before a scan
Straight-beam wall thickness checks on flat plate stock
content.explanation: Side-drilled holes give consistent reflectors at known depths, commonly used to build distance-amplitude references for angle-beam work.
distractors: SDHs are reflectors, not couplant measures.
An SDH is a reference reflector, not a roughness gauge.
An SDH suits angle-beam setup, not flat-plate thickness.

content.stem: Area-amplitude blocks contain flat-bottom holes of different sizes at the same depth to relate:
options: Reflector size to echo amplitude
Reflector depth to echo amplitude
Frequency to the wavelength value
Gain to the sweep range value set
content.explanation: Area-amplitude blocks show how echo amplitude changes with reflector size at a fixed depth, supporting sensitivity reference.
distractors: Varying depth at fixed size is the distance-amplitude block, not the area-amplitude block.
Frequency-to-wavelength is a physics relation, not what these blocks demonstrate.
Gain and sweep range are settings, not what area-amplitude blocks relate.

content.stem: Distance-amplitude blocks contain the same-size reflector at different depths to show how amplitude changes with:
options: Distance (sound path)
The reflector size
The test frequency
The couplant viscosity
content.explanation: These blocks reveal how echo amplitude from an equal reflector falls with depth, the basis for a distance-amplitude correction (DAC) curve.
distractors: Varying size at fixed depth is the area-amplitude block; these vary depth.
Frequency is held constant; depth is the variable here.
Couplant viscosity is not what these blocks demonstrate.

content.stem: A distance-amplitude correction (DAC) curve compensates for the way echo amplitude:
options: Decreases with sound path due to attenuation and beam spread
Increases with sound path as the beam drives deeper down
Tracks only the gain setting and nothing at all about depth
Stays fully constant at every depth right through the part
content.explanation: DAC plots reference reflector amplitude versus distance so equal reflectors at different depths can be judged against a depth-adjusted level.
distractors: Amplitude from an equal reflector generally decreases, not increases, with depth.
DAC addresses depth-related change, not just the gain setting.
Amplitude changes with depth; DAC exists because it is not constant.

content.stem: Straight-beam distance calibration often uses:
options: Backwall echoes from known thicknesses
The initial pulse at the start of sweep
The reject control turned right up high
Random surface echoes off the part
content.explanation: Repeated backwall echoes or steps of known thickness set the sweep so depth reads correctly across the range.
distractors: The initial pulse marks entry; known backwall echoes set the distance scale.
Reject suppresses signals; it does not establish the distance scale.
Calibration uses known reflectors, not random surface echoes.

content.stem: The beam index point (exit point) of an angle-beam probe is found using:
options: A radius on a calibration block such as the IIW
The flat backwall echo off the test part
The width of the initial pulse shown on screen
The reject setting dialed into the unit
content.explanation: Maximizing the echo from the block's machined radius locates where the beam exits the wedge, the beam index point, used for measuring distances.
distractors: A flat backwall does not locate the exit point; a machined radius does.
Initial pulse width does not locate the beam index point.
The reject setting is unrelated to finding the exit point.

content.stem: The actual refracted angle of an angle-beam probe is verified on a:
options: Calibration block with marked angle references
A plain unmarked steel plate with no scale at all
A couplant bottle held up against the probe
The display screen reading by itself
content.explanation: Blocks with angle markings let the technician confirm the true refracted angle, which can differ from the nominal wedge marking, especially as wedges wear.
distractors: An unmarked plate gives no angle reference.
A couplant bottle is not an angle reference.
The display alone does not verify the refracted angle.

content.stem: Calibration standards should have a sound velocity:
options: Matching or representative of the material under test
Far different from the material that is being inspected
Any random value left over from the last test job
Of no real concern at all, since it never affects results
content.explanation: Because depth and sensitivity depend on velocity, the reference material should match or represent the part, or a transfer correction is applied.
distractors: A far-different velocity gives invalid distance and sensitivity.
A random material velocity can invalidate the calibration.
Velocity matching does matter for valid results.

content.stem: Calibration is typically verified:
options: At the start, at intervals, at the end, and when conditions change
Just once a year, and then left alone for the rest of the time
Never, since a good setup holds steady for the entire job
Only right after some indication has been rejected
content.explanation: Procedures require verifying calibration at the start and end of work, at set intervals, and after changes such as a probe, cable, or temperature change.
distractors: Once a year is not adequate for inspection-time validity.
Calibration must be verified, not skipped.
Verification is scheduled, not only after rejections.

content.stem: If a calibration check at the end of a period is out of tolerance, the technician generally must:
options: Recalibrate and reinspect the items checked since the last valid calibration
Ignore the failed check, since the drift only turned up at the very end
Pass the parts on without rechecking any of the work that is done
Drop the gain a little to bring the reading back within tolerance
content.explanation: An out-of-tolerance check means readings since the last good calibration are suspect, so the technician recalibrates and re-examines the affected items per procedure.
distractors: Ignoring a failed check risks accepting invalid results.
Shipping without rechecking is improper.
Simply lowering gain does not address the lost calibration.

content.stem: A large temperature difference between the calibration block and the part can:
options: Shift velocity and readings, requiring correction or on-part calibration
Leave the velocity and the readings completely unchanged the entire time
Permanently change the measured thickness of the actual part tested
Shift the pulse repetition rate that the instrument fires at
content.explanation: Velocity changes with temperature, so calibrating at one temperature and inspecting at a very different one can bias readings unless corrected.
distractors: Temperature does affect velocity and readings.
Temperature does not permanently change the part's thickness.
Temperature does not change the pulse repetition rate.

content.stem: Transfer correction accounts for differences between the calibration block and the part in:
options: Surface condition and attenuation
The part serial number alone
The battery level in the unit
The ambient light in the area
content.explanation: When the part's surface and attenuation differ from the block, a transfer correction adjusts sensitivity so the reference is valid on the actual part.
distractors: The part serial number does not affect the sensitivity transfer.
Battery level is not what transfer correction addresses.
Ambient light does not affect the ultrasonic sensitivity transfer.

content.stem: A two-point thickness calibration sets the:
options: Zero and the velocity/span using two known thicknesses
The receiver gain by itself using a single thickness
The reject and the filter settings on the instrument
The pulse repetition rate set across the unit
content.explanation: Using two known thicknesses lets the gauge set the zero offset and the velocity or span so readings are accurate across the range.
distractors: Gain alone is not a thickness calibration.
Reject and filter settings are not the two-point thickness calibration.
Pulse repetition rate is not set by a two-point thickness calibration.

content.stem: The DSC (distance and sensitivity calibration) block is used for:
options: Angle-beam distance and sensitivity setup in a compact form
Measuring the couplant film thickness held under the probe
Storing the spare probes and wedges away in a tidy way
Setting the display brightness level before any scan begins
content.explanation: The DSC block supports angle-beam distance and sensitivity calibration and angle checks in a compact reference.
distractors: It does not measure couplant.
The DSC block is a calibration reference, not a storage case.
The DSC block sets distance and sensitivity, not brightness.

content.stem: Some calibration blocks let the technician check the instrument and probe:
options: Resolution (ability to separate closely spaced reflectors)
Hardness (the surface toughness of the test metal itself)
Viscosity (the thickness of the couplant gel being applied)
Battery (the charge left in the portable instrument unit)
content.explanation: Resolution checks confirm closely spaced reflectors can be distinguished, an aspect of system performance verified with suitable blocks.
distractors: Hardness is measured with a hardness tester, not a UT resolution block.
Couplant viscosity is a couplant property, not an instrument resolution check.
Battery capacity is not what a resolution block checks.

content.stem: After sensitivity calibration, the reference level and settings are:
options: Recorded so the inspection can be repeated and verified
Changed about freely without writing any of it down
Left at the instrument defaults rather than the procedure
Read off the look of the part rather than any reflector
content.explanation: Recording the reference reflector, level, gain, and settings supports repeatability and later verification.
distractors: Changing settings without recording breaks repeatability.
Defaults are not a substitute for a procedure-set, recorded reference.
The reference is set from a known reflector, not the part's appearance.

content.stem: Many procedures require scanning at a gain above the reference level to:
options: Help detect reflectors that are not perfectly oriented
Cut the overall sensitivity so that the noise drops off
Change the material velocity used right through the part
Drive the couplant film out from under the probe face
content.explanation: A scanning gain above reference improves the chance of catching weak or off-axis indications, which are then evaluated at the reference level.
distractors: Added scanning gain increases, not reduces, sensitivity.
It does not change the material velocity.
It does not remove couplant.

content.stem: Calibration blocks should be:
options: Maintained, identified, and free of damage that affects reflectors
Allowed to corrode and dent, since worn blocks still serve fine
Any random offcut of scrap metal grabbed out of the bin nearby
Painted over the reflectors so as to keep them from rusting up
content.explanation: Damaged or corroded blocks give unreliable references, so they are maintained, controlled, and verified before use.
distractors: Corroded, damaged blocks can give invalid references.
Random scrap is not a controlled reference standard.
Painting over reflectors compromises the block.

content.stem: During calibration, the couplant and coupling should:
options: Match what will be used during inspection
Differ widely from the inspection couplant
Be left off entirely during the calibration
Change at each step of the entire setup
content.explanation: Consistent couplant and coupling between calibration and inspection keep the sensitivity reference valid.
distractors: Large differences can shift the sensitivity reference.
Couplant is required during calibration.
Changing couplant each step undermines consistency.

content.stem: Using backwall multiples from a known thickness helps calibrate the sweep because the echoes are:
options: Evenly spaced at known sound-path intervals
Randomly spaced right across the entire sweep
Color coded by depth across the screen
Fading steadily away after the first echo
content.explanation: Equal spacing of backwall multiples corresponds to known increments of sound path, letting the technician set the horizontal scale accurately.
distractors: The multiples are evenly, not randomly, spaced.
They are not color coded.
Backwall multiples stay evenly spaced; they are real echoes.

content.stem: If the transducer or cable is changed during a job, the technician should:
options: Recalibrate before continuing
Carry straight on with no check
Just nudge the set gain a bit
Leave it be and finish the job
content.explanation: A probe or cable change can shift distance and sensitivity, so calibration is redone before inspection continues.
distractors: Continuing without checking risks invalid readings.
Adjusting gain alone does not re-establish calibration.
The change must be addressed by recalibrating.

content.stem: A DAC curve is built by recording reference echo amplitudes at:
options: Several known distances and connecting them
A single distance read off the sweep screen
A run of random gain settings used on the unit
Several couplant levels under the probe face
content.explanation: Plotting the reference reflector amplitude at several depths and connecting the points forms the DAC used to judge indications by depth.
distractors: A single distance cannot define a distance curve.
DAC is built from amplitudes at known distances, not random gains.
Couplant level does not define DAC points.

content.stem: Reference blocks used for calibration are generally:
options: Controlled and traceable to a recognized standard
Uncontrolled scrap metal kept loose in the truck
Whatever metal happens to be lying around nearby
Thrown out and renewed after each single job
content.explanation: Calibration standards are controlled and, where required, traceable, so the references they provide are reliable.
distractors: Uncontrolled scrap is not a valid standard.
Random nearby metal is not a controlled standard.
Blocks are reused and maintained, not single-use.

content.stem: Calibrating angle-beam distance lets the technician later determine a reflector's:
options: Sound-path, surface, and depth location
The exact type of flaw that it is
The exact size and shape of the reflector
The hardness of the surrounding metal
content.explanation: With distance calibrated, the screen position gives sound path, from which surface distance and depth to a reflector are computed for angle-beam work.
distractors: Calibration gives location, not the flaw type.
Distance calibration gives location, not exact size and shape.
Calibration gives location, not material hardness.

content.stem: In calibration, the Level I technician typically:
options: Performs the calibration to the procedure and records it
Writes the calibration method itself for the others to use
Sets the accept and reject criteria for the entire inspection
Approves the reference standards used across the entire site
content.explanation: A Level I carries out and records the calibration per the procedure under direction; defining methods, criteria, and standards approval are higher-level functions.
distractors: Writing the calibration method is above the Level I.
Acceptance criteria are set above the Level I.
Approving reference standards is above the Level I.

content.stem: Reference reflectors (FBH, SDH, notch) are used because they:
options: Provide known, repeatable echoes to set sensitivity
Are the actual flaws the part carries in service
Soak up the entire beam so that no real echo returns
Amplify the returning echo as it heads back to the screen
content.explanation: Machined reflectors give consistent, known responses so sensitivity can be set and compared the same way every time.
distractors: Reference reflectors are deliberate, known shapes, not the actual flaws.
They reflect sound to give a known echo; they do not absorb the beam.
They are passive references; they do not amplify echoes.

content.stem: A notch in a reference block is often used to set up detection of:
options: Surface-breaking flaws such as cracks, for angle-beam work
Deep rounded porosity buried down within the body of the weld
The grain size of the base metal right across the part
The surface hardness of the metal right under the probe
content.explanation: Notches simulate surface-connected reflectors and help set sensitivity for crack-like flaws in angle-beam inspection.
distractors: A notch simulates surface-connected linear flaws, not deep rounded porosity.
Grain size is a material property, not what a notch sets up.
Hardness is unrelated to setting sensitivity with a notch.

content.stem: A common practice is to recheck calibration at a maximum time interval and whenever:
options: A control is changed or a problem is suspected
Nothing has changed on the entire job
The shift ends at the close of each day
The color of the part shifts during the work
content.explanation: Beyond the time interval, calibration is rechecked after setting changes or if results look suspect, ensuring continued validity.
distractors: Rechecks are tied to time and changes, not the absence of change.
Shift end alone is one trigger, but changes and suspicion also require rechecks.
Part color is not a calibration trigger.

content.stem: If sensitivity is set too low during calibration:
options: Small relevant reflectors may be missed
Heavy background grass floods the screen
The material velocity shifts down lower
The entire sweep range doubles by itself
content.explanation: Under-set sensitivity can leave small reflectors below the reference, risking missed indications, so sensitivity is set per the procedure.
distractors: Heavy background is more associated with excessive gain.
Sensitivity setting does not change material velocity.
Low sensitivity may miss reflectors; it does not change the range.

content.stem: A calibration record typically includes the block, reflectors, settings, and:
options: The technician and date/time
The instrument case color
The probe's resale value
Just a mailing address
content.explanation: Recording who calibrated, when, with what block and settings supports traceability and later verification.
distractors: The instrument color is not part of a calibration record.
Resale value is irrelevant to a calibration record.
An address alone does not document who calibrated and when.

content.stem: Which statement about calibration is correct?
options: Calibrate distance and sensitivity using known reference standards, verify it periodically, and record it
Calibrate the instrument one time only at the very start, then never check it again across the entire job
Set the calibration off any handy bit of scrap metal lying nearby instead of a controlled reference block
Calibration means nothing more than turning the gain up until the backwall echo looks just about right
content.explanation: Calibration sets the distance scale and sensitivity using controlled reference standards, is verified at intervals and on changes, and is recorded for traceability.
distractors: Calibration is verified repeatedly, not once ever.
Controlled, traceable standards are required, not scrap.
Calibration covers distance and sensitivity, not gain alone.

content.stem: Straight-beam (normal-incidence) testing usually uses a:
options: Longitudinal wave directed perpendicular into the part
Refracted shear wave angled in across the test part
Surface wave running along the top face of the part
Radio wave beamed straight down into the part
content.explanation: Straight-beam work sends a longitudinal wave straight into the part, well suited to thickness and laminar (parallel-to-surface) reflectors.
distractors: Refracted shear waves are used in angle-beam work.
Surface waves follow the surface, not straight in.
Radio waves are not ultrasonic.

content.stem: In straight-beam thickness measurement, the key echo is the:
options: Backwall echo from the far surface
Initial pulse at the entry surface
Couplant echo off the gel film
Cable reflection down the lead
content.explanation: The backwall echo time, with the material velocity, gives the thickness. Its position moves with thickness changes.
distractors: The initial pulse marks entry, not thickness.
A couplant echo is not the thickness reference.
Cable reflections are not the thickness measurement.

content.stem: Thickness is computed from:
options: Half the round-trip time multiplied by the material velocity
The full round-trip time multiplied by the material velocity
The echo amplitude multiplied by the set receiver gain value
The test frequency divided straight by the material velocity
content.explanation: Sound travels to the back surface and back, so thickness equals half the round-trip time times velocity.
distractors: The round trip covers twice the thickness, so half the time is used.
Amplitude and gain do not determine thickness; time and velocity do.
Frequency divided by velocity gives a wavelength-related value, not thickness.

content.stem: Several equally spaced echoes on a thin part are typically:
options: Multiple backwall reflections
Several separate small flaws
A run of couplant echoes
Stray cable noise on screen
content.explanation: Sound bouncing between the two surfaces gives evenly spaced backwall multiples, which the technician recognizes rather than counting as flaws.
distractors: Equally spaced repeats are backwall multiples, not separate flaws.
They are backwall echoes, not couplant signals.
They are not cable noise.

content.stem: A lamination in plate often shows as:
options: A mid-wall echo with reduced or lost backwall
A mid-wall echo with a taller backwall behind
No change at all to the usual single backwall echo
A bright color band across the display screen
content.explanation: A lamination parallel to the surface reflects sound at mid-wall and can repeat, while the true backwall weakens or disappears.
distractors: A lamination reduces, not strengthens, the backwall.
A lamination does change the display.
It is an echo, not a color band.

content.stem: Straight-beam testing is best at finding reflectors that are:
options: Parallel to the surface, such as laminations
Standing straight up perpendicular to the surface
Lying right at the outer surface of the part
Tilted steeply away from the incoming sound beam
content.explanation: A straight beam reflects strongly off reflectors facing it (parallel to the surface). Reflectors perpendicular to the surface often need angle-beam work.
distractors: Perpendicular cracks are better found with angle beams.
Straight beam reaches internal reflectors, not only the surface.
Straight beam favors reflectors parallel to the surface, not steeply tilted.

content.stem: A tight crack perpendicular to the surface may be missed by a straight beam because it:
options: Reflects little sound back to the transducer
Speeds the sound up sharply as it passes by
Cannot be detected at any test frequency
Sits below the backwall, out past the thickness
content.explanation: A crack edge-on to a straight beam returns little energy, so angle-beam inspection is used to direct sound across such flaws.
distractors: The issue is reflection geometry; the crack does not speed the sound up.
The crack is missed due to orientation, not because no frequency could detect it.
A through-wall vertical crack is within the thickness, not below the backwall.

content.stem: For thin walls or corroded surfaces, a good choice is a:
options: Dual-element transducer
Large low-frequency probe
A long delay-line probe
A thick single-crystal probe
content.explanation: Dual-element probes reduce the dead zone and handle rough, corroded, or thin walls well, common in corrosion thickness work.
distractors: A large low-frequency single probe is not ideal for thin, corroded walls.
A dual-element probe suits thin and corroded walls better.
A thick single element has poor near-surface resolution for thin walls.

content.stem: Measuring very thin material with a single straight probe is limited by the:
options: Dead zone near the surface
Too strong a backwall echo
The couplant film thickness
The probe cable length
content.explanation: Near-surface echoes can fall in the dead zone of a single probe, so dual-element or delay-line probes are used for thin material.
distractors: A strong backwall is not the limiting factor for thin material.
Couplant thickness is not the dead-zone cause.
Cable length is not the dead-zone cause.

content.stem: On a small-diameter pipe, straight-beam coupling is improved with a:
options: Contoured shoe or proper technique to match the curve
Forcing a flat probe down hard onto the pipe curve
A much higher test frequency to wrap round the pipe curve
Plain dry contact with no couplant on the curve
content.explanation: Matching the probe to the curved surface improves coupling and beam entry, giving more reliable readings than a flat probe rocking on the curve.
distractors: Forcing a flat probe on a curve couples poorly.
Coupling on curved pipe needs a contoured shoe, not higher frequency.
Dry contact leaves a sound-blocking air gap.

content.stem: A digital thickness gauge displays:
options: A numerical thickness value
A surface hardness reading
A refracted angle reading
A couplant viscosity value
content.explanation: Dedicated thickness gauges show a numeric reading (some also show a waveform), calibrated to the material velocity.
distractors: Hardness is measured by a different instrument, not a thickness gauge.
Refracted angle is an angle-beam setup value, not a thickness-gauge readout.
Couplant viscosity is not displayed by a thickness gauge.

content.stem: An incorrect velocity setting in a thickness gauge will:
options: Give an incorrect thickness reading
Leave the thickness reading dead right
Change the couplant used on the surface
Slow the display sweep right down
content.explanation: Thickness scales with velocity, so a wrong velocity yields a wrong thickness even when coupling and echoes are good.
distractors: Velocity errors do affect the reading.
Velocity setting does not change the couplant.
Wrong velocity skews the reading; it does not slow the sweep.

content.stem: To measure metal thickness through a coating, an echo-to-echo mode helps by:
options: Measuring between two backwall echoes to ignore the coating
Measuring from the front surface so the coating is added in
Stripping the metal backwall echoes right out of the reading
Coloring the coating layer apart on the entire display screen
content.explanation: Echo-to-echo measures the interval between successive backwall echoes, which represents the metal and excludes the coating layer.
distractors: Echo-to-echo excludes, rather than adds, the coating.
It uses the metal backwall echoes; it does not remove them.
It does not color the display.

content.stem: If the backwall echo disappears during scanning, the technician should:
options: Investigate for a flaw, lamination, or coupling loss
Take it that the part is perfectly sound right through
Carry on recording and take the loss as quite normal
Change the set velocity until the backwall comes back
content.explanation: A lost backwall can mean a large reflector, lamination, heavy attenuation, or lost coupling, all of which the technician checks.
distractors: A lost backwall is a reason to investigate, not to assume perfection.
Recording continues; the condition is investigated.
Changing velocity does not explain a lost backwall.

content.stem: When scanning an area for thickness or laminations, the technician should:
options: Overlap passes to cover the whole area
Leave gaps between the scanning passes
Read one single point and then move on
Skip the edges of the entire scan area
content.explanation: Overlapping passes ensure full coverage so thinning or laminations are not missed between scan lines.
distractors: Gaps can leave thinning or flaws undetected.
A single point is not full coverage.
Edges are included in the coverage.

content.stem: Scanning too fast can:
options: Cause small indications to be missed
Improve the coverage across the area
Change the material velocity setting
Raise the probe frequency as it runs
content.explanation: Excessive scan speed can skip over small reflectors or thinning, so a controlled speed is used per the procedure.
distractors: Fast scanning hurts, not helps, coverage.
Scan speed does not change material velocity.
Fast scanning may skip indications; it does not change frequency.

content.stem: During straight-beam scanning, a maintained backwall echo helps confirm:
options: Adequate coupling and sound transmission
The exact size of any flaw in the part
An accept or reject call on the entire part
The refracted angle the beam is set to
content.explanation: A steady backwall indicates the sound is entering and returning, a quick check that coupling is adequate as the technician scans.
distractors: A backwall echo confirms coupling, not the size of any flaw.
It indicates sound is passing, not an accept or reject decision.
Refracted angle relates to angle-beam setup, not the straight-beam backwall.

content.stem: Recording thickness readings across a grid to find thinning is called:
options: Corrosion mapping or thickness surveying
Flaw sizing using the angle-beam method
Building a distance-amplitude curve set
Setting the reference sensitivity level up
content.explanation: Taking and recording readings on a grid maps remaining wall thickness to locate corrosion or erosion thinning.
distractors: A thickness grid is corrosion mapping, not angle-beam flaw sizing.
A thickness grid is corrosion mapping, not a DAC plot.
A thickness grid is corrosion mapping, not a sensitivity setup.

content.stem: Very thin sections are challenging because the echoes:
options: Crowd near the initial pulse and can overlap
Spread far apart well clear of one another
Show up along the probe cable instead of the part
Shift in color across the screen instead of crowding
content.explanation: As thickness drops, backwall echoes move close to the initial pulse and can merge, so dual-element or high-frequency delay-line probes are used.
distractors: Thin-section echoes crowd together, not spread apart.
The echoes are in the part, not the cable.
It is a timing issue, not a color change.

content.stem: Before thickness gauging on a rough or scaled surface, the technician should:
options: Prepare the surface enough for good coupling
Leave the loose scale on so as to ease scanning
Read straight through the thick paint as it sits
Skip any preparation at all on the rough surface
content.explanation: Loose scale and roughness scatter sound and disrupt coupling, so the surface is cleaned or conditioned enough for reliable readings.
distractors: Loose scale disrupts coupling and readings.
Thick paint can bias readings unless accounted for.
Some preparation is needed on poor surfaces.

content.stem: Laminations are well detected by straight beam because they are usually:
options: Oriented parallel to the plate surface
Standing up perpendicular to the surface
Found only right at the edge of the plate
Filled with a soft non-metallic paste
content.explanation: Rolling produces laminations parallel to the surface, which face a straight beam and reflect strongly.
distractors: Perpendicular reflectors are harder for a straight beam.
Laminations are within the plate, not only at the edge.
Laminations are flat planar separations, not paste-filled.

content.stem: For consistent straight-beam readings, the couplant film should be:
options: Thin and consistent
Thick and variable
Left off altogether
Just an air gap
content.explanation: A thin, consistent couplant film gives stable coupling and repeatable readings; thick, varying films can shift results.
distractors: Thick, variable films reduce repeatability.
Some couplant is required.
Air does not couple sound into the part.

content.stem: A good practice for an important thickness reading is to:
options: Take repeat readings and confirm coupling and calibration
Take a single reading and write down that one number
Force a number out by running the receiver gain up high
Ignore the backwall echo and read off the gate value alone
content.explanation: Repeating readings and confirming coupling and calibration guards against a one-off coupling or setup error.
distractors: A single reading may hide a coupling error.
Forcing a number with high gain is not valid measurement.
The backwall is central to the measurement.

content.stem: In thin parts, extra small echoes between backwall multiples may be from:
options: Mode-converted or geometry signals the technician must recognize
Sharp cracks in each case, every one a rejectable flaw to mark
A drained battery in the instrument throwing up odd extra spikes
The couplant viscosity throwing the extra echoes onto the screen
content.explanation: Mode conversion and geometry can add small echoes; the technician recognizes them rather than assuming each is a flaw.
distractors: Such echoes are not cracks in every case; they are often mode conversion or geometry.
A drained battery would not create these specific extra echoes.
Couplant viscosity does not create mode-converted echoes.

content.stem: Compared with a flaw detector, a basic thickness gauge is optimized to:
options: Report wall thickness quickly
Build an entire DAC curve set
Size weld flaws by angle beam
Plot a full C-scan image map
content.explanation: Thickness gauges are streamlined for fast, accurate wall readings; full flaw detectors offer the A-scan and controls for flaw work.
distractors: DAC building is a flaw-detector task.
Angle-beam weld sizing is a flaw-detector and higher-level task.
A thickness gauge reads thickness; it does not plot C-scan maps.

content.stem: Thickness readings should be recorded with:
options: Their locations and the relevant settings
Just the bare numbers with no location
Just the room temperature by itself
The color of the instrument's case
content.explanation: Recording where each reading was taken and the setup supports mapping, comparison over time, and traceability.
distractors: Readings without locations lose much of their value.
Temperature alone does not identify where the reading was taken.
The instrument color is not useful record content.

content.stem: Switching from steel to a different alloy for thickness gauging requires:
options: Setting the correct velocity for the new material
No change at all, since the velocity stays the same
Resetting the pulse repetition rate set on the unit
Fitting a larger probe to suit the different alloy
content.explanation: Each material has its own velocity, so the gauge is set to the correct value before measuring the new material.
distractors: A different material has a different velocity, so a change is required.
Pulse repetition rate does not correct for a different material velocity.
Probe size alone does not address the velocity difference.

content.stem: On hot piping, thickness readings can be affected by temperature, so the technician:
options: Uses high-temperature gear and applies any required correction
Takes the readings as they come and ignores the heat altogether
Ices the probe down first to hold it cool against the pipe
Turns the gauge right off whenever the pipe runs far too hot
content.explanation: High-temperature probes and couplants and a temperature correction keep hot-service readings valid.
distractors: Temperature can bias readings and is not ignored.
Icing the probe is not the proper method.
Turning off the gauge does not take a reading.

content.stem: For lamination checks on plate before welding, the technician scans:
options: The area to be welded and adjacent zones per procedure
One single random spot somewhere out on the plate
Only the outer edge of the plate, nothing inside it
None of it at all, since the plate is taken as sound
content.explanation: Scanning the weld-prep area and adjacent material per the procedure ensures laminations that could affect the weld are found.
distractors: A single random spot is not adequate coverage.
Only the edge misses interior laminations.
The check must actually be performed.

content.stem: In straight-beam and thickness work, the Level I technician:
options: Takes and records readings and indications under direction
Sets the remaining-life limits for the entire piping run
Approves the entire inspection plan before the work starts
Decides the disposition of the component right on the spot
content.explanation: A Level I performs measurements and records results; setting criteria, approving plans, and dispositioning are higher-level responsibilities.
distractors: Remaining-life criteria are set above the Level I.
Approving the plan is above the Level I.
Component disposition is above the Level I scope.

content.stem: A sudden very low thickness reading should be:
options: Verified for coupling, peak jumping, and an interim reflector before accepting
Written straight into the record as the true wall thickness with no check at all
Put down to a thick paint layer and then left at that without looking further
Taken as a quirk of the gauge and passed over without any further thought
content.explanation: Spurious low readings can come from poor coupling, peak jumping to an earlier signal, or the gauge locking onto a mid-wall reflector such as a lamination, so the technician verifies before recording a critical value.
distractors: A critical reading is verified, not recorded blindly.
It should be checked, not assumed to be paint.
An anomalous reading is investigated, not ignored.

content.stem: Which statement about straight-beam and thickness work is correct?
options: A straight longitudinal beam measures thickness from the backwall and finds laminar reflectors
A straight beam is the best way of all to catch tight cracks that stand up across the wall
The velocity setting makes no difference at all to the thickness that the gauge reports
Coupling quality has no real bearing on the readings that a thickness gauge gives at all
content.explanation: Straight-beam UT uses the backwall echo and velocity to measure thickness and is well suited to laminar reflectors, with correct velocity and consistent coupling essential.
distractors: Vertical cracks usually need angle-beam inspection.
Velocity setting directly affects thickness readings.
Coupling strongly affects readings.

content.stem: Angle-beam inspection in steel typically introduces a:
options: Refracted shear wave at a known angle
Straight longitudinal wave straight in
Surface wave along the top part face
Radio wave beamed into the part
content.explanation: A wedge refracts and mode-converts the sound so a shear wave travels into the part at a known angle, used for welds and similar geometries.
distractors: A straight longitudinal wave is straight-beam, not angle-beam.
Surface waves are a different mode for surface flaws.
Radio waves are not ultrasonic.

content.stem: The beam index point is the location where the:
options: Sound beam exits the wedge into the part
The probe cable joins onto the connector
The couplant gel sits under the probe face
The beam strikes the far backwall surface
content.explanation: The beam index point (exit point) is where the beam leaves the wedge; distances to reflectors are measured from it.
distractors: The cable connection is not the beam index point.
Couplant location is not the beam index point.
The backwall is the far surface, not the exit point.

content.stem: The refracted angle is used along with sound path to determine a reflector's:
options: Surface distance and depth
Its full length and its width
The flaw type and severity
The metal grade and hardness
content.explanation: Knowing the angle and the sound path lets the technician compute how far along the surface and how deep a reflector lies.
distractors: Angle-beam location gives distance and depth, not size.
It gives location, not flaw type or severity.
It gives location, not material grade.

content.stem: In angle-beam work, a leg is the portion of the sound path:
options: Between reflections off the surfaces (for example first leg to the backwall)
Running back along the probe cable from the connector right to the wedge face
Sitting within the couplant film held in between the wedge and the part
Travelling out in the air beyond the far edges of the part being scanned
content.explanation: The beam travels in legs, reflecting between the surfaces. The first leg reaches the far surface; the second leg continues after that reflection.
distractors: A leg is in the part, not the cable.
A leg is in the part, not the couplant.
Legs are within the part, not outside it.

content.stem: The skip distance relates to the angle and the part thickness and describes the:
options: Surface distance for the beam to complete a full V-path
Depth below the surface at which a given reflector lies
Thickness of the wedge mounted beneath the element
Width of the element fitted within the probe case
content.explanation: Skip distance is the surface distance over which the beam goes down and back up (a full V), used to plan transducer positions for full coverage.
distractors: Skip distance is a surface distance, not the depth of a reflector.
The wedge thickness is not the skip distance.
Element width is not the skip distance.

content.stem: Inspecting a weld, the technician uses first-leg and second-leg positions to:
options: Cover the weld volume from root to cap
Cover only the cap face at the weld top
Measure the plate thickness at the weld
Set the reject level used for the scan
content.explanation: Moving the probe toward and away from the weld places the beam at different legs so the full cross-section, root through cap, is examined.
distractors: Using both legs covers the full volume, not only the cap surface.
Leg positions are for coverage, not just thickness measurement.
Reject level is an instrument setting, not the purpose of leg positions.

content.stem: To evaluate a reflector with an angle beam, the technician:
options: Manipulates the probe to maximize the echo, then notes its position
Takes the very first glimpse of the echo and writes that down at once
Moves the probe to bury the indication down in the baseline noise
Wipes the couplant off so that the echo settles to a steady height
content.explanation: Rotating and moving the probe to peak the signal gives the best response and helps locate the reflector accurately.
distractors: Peaking the signal by movement is needed, not just the first glimpse.
Hiding the indication defeats the inspection.
Removing couplant loses the signal.

content.stem: A common angle-beam weld scanning motion combines:
options: Advancing along the weld while moving toward and away from it
Running one straight line along the full length of the weld
Holding the probe dead still over a single spot on the weld
Sweeping only across the cap face and never down to the root
content.explanation: The technician advances along the weld while oscillating toward and away, often with rotation, to cover the volume and catch various flaw orientations.
distractors: A single straight line misses much of the volume.
Holding still does not scan the weld.
Only scanning the cap misses the root and body.

content.stem: Welds are typically scanned with the angle beam from:
options: Both sides and in both directions where access allows
One side only, in a single set direction along the weld
The cap surface only, with no side-to-side scan at all
One single fixed spot, with no movement along the weld
content.explanation: Scanning from both sides and directions improves the chance of crossing flaws of different orientations and covering the whole weld.
distractors: One side may miss flaws favoring the other direction.
Cap-only scanning is not full coverage.
Access permitting, both surfaces and sides are used.

content.stem: Transfer correction in angle-beam work adjusts for differences between the calibration block and the part in:
options: Surface roughness and attenuation
The weld length and the total run
The ambient temperature alone
The transducer serial number
content.explanation: When the part surface and attenuation differ from the block, a transfer correction keeps the sensitivity reference valid on the part.
distractors: Weld length is not what transfer correction addresses.
Ambient temperature alone is not the basis for transfer correction.
The transducer serial number does not affect the sensitivity transfer.

content.stem: In weld scanning, echoes from the root, cap, or counterbore are:
options: Geometry signals the technician must recognize, not automatically flaws
Always real flaws to be marked and rejected without any further look
Echoes thrown off the couplant film held in under the moving probe face
Stray noise carried in along the probe cable from a loose connector end
content.explanation: Weld geometry produces predictable echoes; the technician learns to recognize these so they are not confused with flaw indications.
distractors: Geometry echoes are not automatically flaws.
They are weld-geometry echoes, not couplant echoes.
They are not cable noise.

content.stem: The points where the angle beam reflects off a surface are sometimes called:
options: Nodes (skip points)
Wet couplant points
Probe cable nodes
Bright color points
content.explanation: Node or skip points are where the beam meets a surface and reflects; knowing their locations helps plan coverage and interpret signals.
distractors: They are beam reflection points, not couplant points.
They are not cable nodes.
They are not color points.

content.stem: Before angle-beam scanning, the technician:
options: Verifies the index point, angle, distance, and sensitivity
Skips the calibration and gets straight on with the scanning
Checks only the battery charge left in the handheld unit
Notes down the surface color of the entire part being scanned
content.explanation: Angle-beam setup confirms the beam index point, refracted angle, distance calibration, and reference sensitivity before inspection.
distractors: Calibration is required before scanning, not skipped.
Battery level alone is not the angle-beam setup.
Part color is not part of the angle-beam setup.

content.stem: As an angle-beam wedge wears, the technician should expect the:
options: Index point and refracted angle to shift, requiring recheck
Operating frequency of the element to double up on each shot
Color of the couplant gel to change right under the probe face
Length of the probe cable to stretch right out over the job
content.explanation: Wedge wear moves the exit point and can change the refracted angle, so these are rechecked periodically and after heavy use.
distractors: Wedge wear does not double the frequency.
It does not change couplant color.
It does not lengthen the cable.

content.stem: From the sound path and refracted angle, the surface distance to a reflector is found using the:
options: Geometry of the angle (a trigonometric relationship)
Height of the echo shown on the screen at the time
Pulse repetition rate set across the instrument unit
Viscosity of the couplant gel held under the probe
content.explanation: Surface distance and depth follow from the sound path and angle by trigonometry, which the technician applies or reads from a calculator or chart.
distractors: Amplitude does not give the surface distance; the angle geometry does.
Pulse repetition rate is unrelated to locating the reflector.
Couplant viscosity does not determine surface distance.

content.stem: A reflector found in the second leg is located by accounting for the:
options: Reflection off the far surface (using the skip geometry)
Height of the initial pulse over at the left of the sweep
Test frequency that the transducer is set to run at
Viscosity of the couplant gel under the moving probe face
content.explanation: Second-leg reflectors are above the far surface in the return path, so the depth is computed from the skip geometry, not read as a simple first-leg depth.
distractors: The initial pulse amplitude does not locate a second-leg reflector.
Frequency does not change the second-leg geometry.
Couplant viscosity is unrelated to the second-leg location.

content.stem: Different refracted angles are used to:
options: Better intersect flaws of different orientations and weld bevels
Stretch out the battery life of the handheld instrument on site
Take up the slack in the probe cable across a long job run
Change the pulse repetition rate that the unit fires at
content.explanation: Choosing 45, 60, or 70 degrees helps the beam strike flaws and fusion faces more squarely depending on the joint geometry.
distractors: Angle choice does not affect battery life.
Angle choice does not change the cable.
Angle choice is about flaw orientation, not pulse repetition rate.

content.stem: Angle-beam scanning needs couplant that:
options: Maintains coupling as the probe moves over the surface
Dries off at once the very moment it touches the surface
Is left off entirely throughout the contact scanning
Is just the air gap kept between the probe and part
content.explanation: A suitable couplant maintains a consistent film as the probe is manipulated, keeping sensitivity stable during scanning.
distractors: Instant drying would break coupling during scanning.
Couplant is required for contact angle-beam work.
Air does not couple the sound.

content.stem: Mode-converted or geometry echoes during angle-beam scanning can:
options: Appear as indications the technician must correctly identify
Never show up at all during any properly run angle-beam scan
Show up only in straight-beam work, never in angle-beam
Always stand taller than every real flaw echo on the screen
content.explanation: Angle-beam work can show mode-converted and geometry signals; recognizing them prevents false calls and missed real flaws.
distractors: Such echoes do appear and must be recognized.
They occur in angle-beam work, not only straight-beam.
They are not always stronger than real flaw echoes.

content.stem: When an angle-beam indication is found, the technician records its:
options: Position, sound path, and amplitude relative to reference
Length, width, and through-wall height to the nearest unit
Flaw type, severity, and the likely cause of the indication
Probe angle, gain setting, and the couplant brand used
content.explanation: Recording where the indication is, its sound path or depth, and its amplitude versus reference supports later evaluation.
distractors: A Level I records position and amplitude, not reflector size.
Judging type and cause is above the Level I record.
Those are setup details, not the indication's recorded data.

content.stem: Angle-beam scan passes should overlap to:
options: Ensure the full weld volume is covered
Save on couplant gel across the long run
Cut right down the coverage over the weld
Steer well clear of the weld root region
content.explanation: Overlapping passes prevent gaps so the entire weld cross-section is examined.
distractors: Overlap is about coverage, not saving couplant.
Overlap increases, not reduces, coverage.
The root must be covered, not avoided.

content.stem: A straight beam is often inadequate for weld cracks because the cracks are:
options: Frequently oriented so a straight beam reflects little from them
Always lying flat and parallel to the outer plate surface above
Always sitting right at the outer surface of the weld joint itself
Buried very deep down near the root of the thick welded joint
content.explanation: Many weld flaws are oriented such that a straight beam misses them, so an angled shear beam is directed to strike them more squarely.
distractors: Weld cracks are not always parallel to the surface.
Weld flaws are not always at the surface.
Straight beam misses cracks by orientation, not by their depth.

content.stem: Angle-beam sensitivity is commonly set using:
options: Side-drilled holes or notches in a reference block
The part's own backwall echo and nothing else besides
The height of the initial pulse shown over at the left
Whatever surface reflector turns up first on the part
content.explanation: Side-drilled holes and notches provide repeatable reflectors at known depths to set angle-beam reference sensitivity, sometimes forming a DAC.
distractors: The part's backwall alone is not the angle-beam sensitivity reference.
Initial pulse height is not used to set angle-beam sensitivity.
Known reference reflectors are used, not random surface reflectors.

content.stem: During a long angle-beam job, sensitivity and calibration are:
options: Rechecked at intervals and after changes
Set just one time at the very start
Left ignored across the entire long job
Changed about at random through the work
content.explanation: Periodic rechecks and rechecks after probe, cable, or temperature changes keep the inspection valid.
distractors: A single setup is not enough for a long job.
Calibration is not ignored.
Settings are controlled, not random.

content.stem: Good angle-beam coverage requires the scanning surface to be:
options: Prepared so the probe couples and moves smoothly
Left heavy with scale to help the probe slide
Coated in thick paint to seal it before scanning
Of any condition at all, since it makes no difference
content.explanation: A reasonably clean, smooth surface lets the probe couple and slide for consistent angle-beam scanning.
distractors: Heavy scale disrupts coupling and movement.
Thick paint can disrupt coupling and beam entry.
Surface condition does matter.

content.stem: After locating and recording an angle-beam indication, evaluation against acceptance criteria is:
options: Generally a Level II or III responsibility
Squarely within the Level I scope of the work
Left out entirely once the entire scan is done
Based on the loudest echo seen on the screen
content.explanation: A Level I detects, locates, and records; sizing and accepting or rejecting against the code is normally a higher-level task.
distractors: Acceptance evaluation is above the Level I scope.
Evaluation is required, not skipped.
Acceptance is judged against criteria, not simply the loudest echo.

content.stem: On pipe welds, a contoured wedge is used so the angle beam:
options: Couples and enters at the intended angle on the curved surface
Skips right past the weld and reads the clear pipe wall nearby
Turns into a straight beam running square down into the pipe wall
Removes any need to calibrate before the pipe weld is scanned
content.explanation: A wedge contoured to the pipe maintains coupling and the intended refracted angle on the curved surface.
distractors: The goal is to inspect, not skip, the weld.
It remains an angle beam, not a straight beam.
Calibration is still required.

content.stem: Marking skip distances on the part helps the technician:
options: Position the probe for first-leg and second-leg coverage
Change the material velocity set right through the part
Change the operating frequency of the transducer fitted
Change the measured thickness of the entire part being scanned
content.explanation: Reference marks for skip distances guide probe placement so the weld is covered in the appropriate legs.
distractors: Marking distances does not change the material velocity.
It does not change the transducer frequency.
It does not change the part thickness.

content.stem: An angle-beam indication's significance is first gauged by comparing its amplitude with the:
options: Reference level (for example DAC or a set percent of screen)
Initial pulse height over at the far left of the entire sweep line
Scanning speed that the probe is moved across the weld at
Transducer serial number printed on the side of the probe case
content.explanation: Indications are compared with the reference sensitivity (such as a DAC curve or set screen height) to decide what is recorded and passed for evaluation.
distractors: The initial pulse height is not the evaluation reference.
Scanning speed affects coverage, not the amplitude reference.
The transducer serial number is not a reference level.

content.stem: In angle-beam scanning, the Level I technician:
options: Scans, locates, and records indications under direction
Sizes the flaws and sets disposition to the governing code
Approves the inspection procedures used right across the site
Sets the accept and reject criteria for the entire weld job
content.explanation: A Level I performs the scanning and records indications; sizing, disposition, procedure approval, and criteria are higher-level functions.
distractors: Sizing and disposition to code are above the Level I.
Approving procedures is above the Level I.
Setting acceptance criteria is above the Level I.

content.stem: To help judge whether an angle-beam echo is from a real reflector, the technician can:
options: Move the probe and observe how the signal behaves with position
Treat every echo on screen as a real flaw without any check
Switch the instrument right off and read off the last frozen trace
Hold the probe dead still and never shift it off that one spot
content.explanation: How a signal moves and changes with probe position helps distinguish real reflectors from geometry or spurious signals, before evaluation.
distractors: Not every echo is a flaw; behavior is assessed.
Turning off the instrument does not assess the signal.
Probe position is key to interpreting the signal.

content.stem: Which statement about angle-beam scanning is correct?
options: A refracted shear beam covers the weld in legs, with reflectors located from sound path and angle
Angle-beam work fires a straight longitudinal wave square into the part and reads off the backwall
Weld root and cap geometry never throw any echo that might be taken for a real flaw at all
Sizing each weld flaw to the governing code is a routine part of the Level I scope of the work
content.explanation: Angle-beam UT uses a refracted shear wave, covers welds in first and second legs, and locates reflectors from sound path and angle, with evaluation left to higher levels.
distractors: Angle beam uses a refracted shear wave, not a straight longitudinal wave.
Weld geometry does cause recognizable echoes.
Sizing flaws to code is above the Level I scope.

content.stem: When an indication is found, the Level I technician records its:
options: Location, amplitude, and sound path or depth
Length, width, and through-wall height in units
Flaw type, the cause, and a severity rating
Probe angle, the gain, and the couplant brand
content.explanation: Recording where the indication is, how strong it is versus reference, and its depth or sound path supports later evaluation and traceability.
distractors: A Level I records location and amplitude, not reflector size.
Judging type, cause, and severity is above the Level I record.
Those are setup details, not the indication's recorded data.

content.stem: A UT record typically identifies the part, procedure, equipment, settings, technician, and:
options: Date and calibration details
The weather on the day
The resale value of the part
Just a phone number
content.explanation: Capturing the date and calibration details ties the results to a known setup and supports traceability and repeatability.
distractors: Weather is not the needed identifying detail for a UT record.
Resale value is irrelevant to a UT record.
A phone number alone does not document the date and calibration.

content.stem: Vertical (amplitude) linearity checks confirm the display responds:
options: Proportionally to changes in echo amplitude
With a color shift as echo amplitude changes
By tracking the couplant film below the probe
At random with no link to the echo amplitude
content.explanation: Vertical linearity verifies that screen height changes in proportion to input amplitude, so amplitude-based evaluation is valid.
distractors: Linearity is about amplitude response, not color.
It is not about couplant.
A linear display responds proportionally, not randomly.

content.stem: Horizontal (distance) linearity checks confirm that:
options: Screen positions correspond accurately to sound path or depth
Echo height responds in proportion to the size of the reflector
Battery charge holds steady right through the entire inspection
Couplant color stays even across the entire surface of the part
content.explanation: Horizontal linearity verifies the sweep represents distance accurately, so reflector positions and thickness are correct.
distractors: Amplitude response is vertical linearity, not horizontal.
Battery charge is not what horizontal linearity verifies.
Couplant color is unrelated to distance linearity.

content.stem: Instrument linearity checks are:
options: Performed at required intervals, sometimes by the Level I under direction
Skipped over entirely, since a working instrument is taken as good enough
Run purely as a marketing claim with no real bearing on the performance
Carried out by the part supplier rather than by qualified inspection staff
content.explanation: Linearity is checked on a schedule to keep the instrument valid; a Level I may perform routine checks and record them under direction.
distractors: Linearity checks are required, not skipped.
They are a real performance check, not marketing.
They are done by qualified personnel, not the part supplier.

content.stem: Calibration verification intervals during inspection exist to:
options: Catch drift before it invalidates results
Add a set delay between the scanning runs
Stand in for the written procedure itself
Set the accept and reject criteria in use
content.explanation: Periodic verification catches setup drift so readings stay valid, with reinspection of affected items if a check fails.
distractors: The purpose is validity, not arbitrary delay.
Verification supports, not replaces, the procedure.
It does not set acceptance criteria.

content.stem: Consistent couplant use is a process control because changes can:
options: Shift signal amplitude and affect readings
Alter the measured wall thickness reading
Change the probe operating frequency set
Heat the entire part surface under the probe
content.explanation: Because coupling affects amplitude, consistent couplant and technique between calibration and inspection keep results valid.
distractors: Couplant changes affect amplitude, not the true wall thickness.
Couplant changes affect amplitude, not the probe frequency.
Couplant changes affect amplitude, not the part temperature.

content.stem: Surface temperature is controlled in UT because it can affect:
options: Couplant performance and sound velocity
The brightness of the display screen view
The gain setting stored in the instrument
The model name printed on the gauge case
content.explanation: Temperature changes velocity and can degrade standard couplants, so limits and high-temperature gear are used as required.
distractors: Temperature affects couplant and velocity, not screen brightness.
Temperature affects couplant and velocity, not the stored gain.
Temperature affects couplant and velocity, not the printed model name.

content.stem: A safety characteristic of UT is that it:
options: Produces no ionizing radiation
Emits a weak ionizing radiation dose
Needs a posted radiation area
Requires film badge monitoring
content.explanation: UT uses sound and emits no ionizing radiation, avoiding the radiation hazards and controls of radiography.
distractors: UT does not emit gamma rays.
UT does not require a radiation area.
Film badges are a radiography control, not needed for UT sound.

content.stem: In immersion UT, a key safety consideration is:
options: Electrical safety around water and equipment
Hearing protection from the loud water pump motor
Explosive gas buildup over the water bath
Eye strain from the bright tank display screen
content.explanation: Combining water with electrical equipment requires proper grounding, GFCI protection, and care to prevent shock hazards.
distractors: The key immersion concern is electrical safety around water, not pump noise.
Explosive gas is not an inherent immersion-UT hazard.
The key concern is electrical safety around water, not eye strain.

content.stem: Automated scanning equipment introduces hazards such as:
options: Moving parts and pinch points
Bright flashing display images
Strong couplant gel odors given off
Static buildup on the screen
content.explanation: Scanners and manipulators have moving parts, so guarding and awareness prevent pinch and entanglement injuries.
distractors: Scanner hazards are mechanical, not screen flashes.
Couplant odor is minor; the hazard is moving parts.
Screen static is not the mechanical scanner hazard.

content.stem: Spilled couplant on the floor is a:
options: Slip hazard that should be cleaned up
Setup step that the job plan calls for
Harmless residue that can be left alone
A handy marker for where to scan next
content.explanation: Couplant spills are slippery; cleaning them up and managing waste maintain a safe, orderly work area.
distractors: A spill is a hazard, not a requirement.
Spilled couplant is a slip hazard, not harmless residue.
Spilled couplant is a slip hazard, not a scan marker.

content.stem: The Level I technician performs UT according to:
options: The written procedure and instructions
Whatever personal preference suits
Whatever runs fastest on the job
Memory of some past different job
content.explanation: Work follows the qualified written procedure so results are valid and repeatable, with questions referred to higher-level personnel.
distractors: Personal preference is not the basis for the method.
Speed does not override the procedure.
A different job's memory does not govern this inspection.

content.stem: Inspection results should be reported:
options: Accurately and completely to the responsible personnel
By word of mouth only, with nothing put in writing
Adjusted to pass first before they are handed over
As a bare pass or fail with no supporting data at all
content.explanation: Accurate, complete records are provided to the responsible parties; results are never altered, and data is retained per requirements.
distractors: A verbal-only report leaves no traceable record.
Altering results to pass is falsification.
A bare pass with no data does not support traceability or review.

content.stem: UT personnel typically must meet a vision requirement for:
options: Near vision, to read the display and records
Color vision alone, with no near-vision check
No vision standard required for the work
Distance vision only, across the wide shop
content.explanation: Reading the display and documentation requires adequate near vision, verified per the written practice and rechecked periodically.
distractors: Near vision is required, beyond color alone.
Vision requirements do apply to NDT personnel.
Near vision, not only distance vision, is relevant.

content.stem: If a reading looks unfavorable, the technician should:
options: Record it accurately and refer evaluation to the proper level
Change the figure so the part comes out acceptable on the paper
Delete the unfavorable reading and move along to the next spot
Round the reading off until the part just scrapes through a pass
content.explanation: Data is recorded truthfully; evaluation against criteria is done by qualified personnel. Altering data is falsification.
distractors: Changing data to look acceptable is falsification.
Deleting unfavorable data is improper.
Rounding to pass is falsification.

content.stem: Recording the gain, reference level, and probe used allows the inspection to be:
options: Repeated and verified later
Billed out to the client
Run with no probe fitted
Set at random every time
content.explanation: Documenting the setup supports repeating and verifying the inspection and comparing results over time.
distractors: Recording settings supports repeatability, not billing.
A probe is required; records do not remove that need.
The point of recording settings is consistent, not random, sensitivity.

content.stem: When an indication needs sizing or acceptance decisions, the Level I:
options: Refers it to a Level II or III
Decides on acceptance itself
Ignores it and carries on
Wipes it off the record
content.explanation: Sizing and acceptance are higher-level tasks, so the Level I records the indication and refers it for evaluation.
distractors: Acceptance decisions are above the Level I.
Indications are referred, not ignored.
Indications are kept in the record, not removed.

content.stem: Routine equipment and calibration checks should be:
options: Recorded so the instrument's validity is documented
Run but left off the record, as they are routine
Skipped over to save time on a busy inspection shift
Kept in memory rather than written down at all
content.explanation: Recording checks documents that the instrument was valid during the work, supporting traceability.
distractors: Undocumented checks leave validity unproven.
Skipping checks risks invalid results.
Memory is not a substitute for recorded checks.

content.stem: Appropriate UT safety practice includes:
options: Following site PPE and electrical and mechanical safety rules
Skipping the site safety rules whenever the schedule runs tight
Pulling the machine guards right off to reach the work faster
Stepping into restricted areas without any clearance first
content.explanation: UT work follows general site safety, including PPE, electrical safety (especially immersion), and machine guarding around scanners.
distractors: Site rules are followed, not ignored.
Guards stay in place for safety.
Restricted areas require proper clearance.

content.stem: UT records are generally:
options: Retained per the applicable requirements
Thrown out the moment the scan ends
Kept on only when it suits the work crew
Never even written up in the first place
content.explanation: Records are kept for the required retention period so results can be reviewed and verified later.
distractors: Records are retained, not discarded immediately.
Retention is a requirement, not a convenience.
Records are created as part of the inspection.

content.stem: Documenting settings and calibration supports repeatability, which means:
options: Another technician can reproduce the inspection and results
The original results can never be checked back over again
No later inspection can confirm the figures taken
The records are held back from the responsible parties
content.explanation: Repeatability lets the inspection be reproduced and verified, a core reason for thorough records.
distractors: Good records make results checkable, not uncheckable.
Documentation makes inspections verifiable, not unverifiable.
Records are shared with responsible parties, not hidden.

content.stem: If the instrument fails a linearity or calibration check, the technician should:
options: Stop, address the fault, and re-examine affected work
Carry on regardless and finish the entire scan as planned
Leave the failure off the record and just press ahead
Wind the gain right up until the check seems to pass
content.explanation: A failed check means results may be invalid, so the cause is corrected and affected items are re-examined per procedure.
distractors: Continuing on a faulty instrument risks invalid results.
The failure and actions are documented, not omitted.
Raising gain does not fix a linearity or calibration fault.

content.stem: Couplant should be chosen so it is:
options: Compatible with the part and safe to handle
Strongly corrosive against the part surface
Highly flammable around the entire work area
Toxic to any technician who handles it
